subtopic: PAYMENTS UNDER GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
PAYMENTS UNDER GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, that being the government's reluctance to pay out moneys owing to Canadian farmers under the grain stabilization plan. The amount of the payment is known to be in the range of $80 million to $95 million, and the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to the effect that the cabinet must consider the final figures is utter nonsense and means nothing more than fixing the date of payment in relation to the timing of the upcoming election. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That the money owing to western grain farmers under the grain stabilization program be paid out immediately and not be subjected to the political manipulations of the Minister of Agriculture and the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board.

speechtext:

That this House congratulate the NFB and the directors and crews involved for this outstanding achievement.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REDUCTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced yesterday that he will soon bring forward a budget, and that in a period of economic crisis; given also that according to the report of the National Welfare Council the income gap between the rich and the poor increases continuously, and that in 1976 it was two and a half times as large as in 1951, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House direct the Minister of Finance to introduce in his budget a series of measures such as tax reductions, the exclusion from taxation of government pension plans and a real annual guaranteed income plan.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF DEPARTMENT TO ALLOW WOMAN TO UNDERGO PILOT TRAINING-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the refusal of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) to allow Julia Walsh, a young woman from Ajax, Ontario, to apply for the Canadian armed forces pilot training program because, in the words of the Canadian armed forces recruiting officer, "young ladies are not eligible to apply for pilot training", considering the minister's rejection of my appeal on her behalf, and further considering the subsequent decision by the chief human rights commissioner of Canada to support Miss Walsh and help remove the unfair impediment to her becoming a Canadian armed forces trainee, contrary to the provisions of section 2 of the Human Rights Act, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House urges the Minister of National Defence to accept Julia Walsh and other qualified women candidates as applicants for pilot training and support, rather than retard, the movement toward equality of opportunity for both men and women.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT CAN AFFORD INCREASED EXPENDITURES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in Sherbrooke, Quebec, on March 13, 1978, that the government must be able to afford increased expenditures, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That the minister make a statement to the House making it clear whether or not she knew that the government would, as of now, require to borrow another $1 billion for use as standby credit, whether or not she had given consideration to the pending $11 billion cash requirement of the government this year, and whether or not the extra money required would be derived from increased taxation or a further budgetary deficit.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL OF GOVERNMENT TO STOCKPILE NICKEL-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the federal government has refused over the last few months to consider the stockpiling of nickel as a move to protect nickel mining communities and the jobs of miners, in view of the fact that Inco last week raised the price of nickel by 7 per cent a pound in a move which may be the start of a recovery in that industry, and bearing in mind the fact that if the government had acquired a one-month inventory of 30 million pounds of nickel to protect the jobs of miners they would now be in the position of having made an inventory profit of over $2 million, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes):
That this House condemn the short-sighted policies of this government which have not only cost over 4,000 jobs in this industry but which have cost Canadian taxpayers $2 million because the government lost an opportunity to make a profit on Canadian resources.

subtopic: EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Has the government any reason to believe that the Economic Council of Canada, which will monitor price and wage performance after controls are lifted on April 14, will be any more successful in obtaining compliance with the government's price and wage guidelines than was the Prices and Incomes Commission under the chairmanship of Dr. John Young, which proved to be completely incapable of doing so? If so, what are the government's reasons for so believing?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since that appeared in the early seventies we have reached two-digit inflation. Co-operation was forthcoming from the private sector during the period in which we had controls. It is obvious there was a great deal of co-operation from the private sector because they realized the danger of runaway inflation. Because of this, we are quite convinced that the private sector and the government, as employers, will be very, very serious in their undertaking to control any inflationary spiralling.

subtopic: EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course, that is pure speculation. The Prime Minister avoided answering a serious economic question, as he always does. I have a supplementary question for him. Does the Prime Minister not realize that without teeth to require compliance with the government's guidelines, the pressures that have built up on prices and wages during the past 2Vi years will bring about an even greater price escalation than that which necessitated the imposition of controls in the first place?

subtopic: EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I point out to the hon. gentleman that it is not, to use his words, pure speculation: it is based on an agreement reached between the ten provincial premiers and myself, when we met in mid-February, to act as employers in a way which would keep any upward pressure on the public sector within the same range as that of the private sector. That is not speculation: it is an agreement set out by the ten premiers and myself in the communique issued at the end of the conference.

subtopic: EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister not realize that this is not a matter which can be settled by the ten premiers but, rather, by the heads of labour and management in this country? There has been no agreement whatsoever among labour, management and the government to keep prices and wages down. Therefore, does he not realize that we are right back to where we were when the government, in 1969, formed the Prices and Incomes Commission; and does he not realize that we are headed on the same disastrous course?

subtopic: EEC MONITORING OF PRICES AND WAGES
speechtext:
I think the fact which escapes the hon. member is that the governments in this country-federal, provincial and municipal-are also employers, and when they undertake to follow a certain line of conduct as employers, this is certainly a very important advance in attempting to control the inflationary spiral. Beyond that, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter for the hon. gentleman opposite to have confidence in the ability of the provinces to deliver on their word.
As far as we are concerned, there is a bill before the House now, the Public Service Staff Relations Act, dealing with amendments which we invite the opposition to vote for, and thereby give the government the power to make sure that it does stay within a reasonable escalation of wages. I await the support of the opposition for the government to deliver on its undertaking.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO IMPROVE SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Postmaster General. Mr. Speaker, when we in this party speak of equality, we do not try to equalize all citizens and lower the incomes of upper income people to a very low average. speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I should like to begin by drawing attention to question No. 1,085 which was placed on the order paper on January 23 and which has not as yet been answered. In doing so I should like to thank the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamon-tagne) for sending me the answer which should, actually, have been tabled in the House. I cannot understand how such a thing could happen, but it happened. Here is the answer which should have been given in the House some time ago. What is even more interesting is the fact that the reply bears a departmental notation which reads as follows: "There is a time limit of ten working days for preparing replies to written

questions." The notation then goes on to say other things concerning steps to be taken if an extension of time is required, and so on. The note is signed by Ronald Regimbald, Public Affairs Branch, Parliamentary Returns.
Mr. Speaker, if there is a ten-day limit on preparing replies to questions put down by members of this House, I think I am justified in asking why question No. 44 which was originally placed on the order paper on December 20, 1976-one year and four months ago-concerning a letter sent by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to all members of the Liberal party in this House, has not been answered, bearing, as it does, upon his use of government aircraft.
I draw attention, also, to three further questions which are in a similar category, first, No. 45, placed on the order paper one year and two months ago on February 7, 1977, concerning the massive fingerprinting operation carried out on public servants; the government will not disclose the number of those who have been fingerprinted, but it runs into thousands and thousands and involves an invasion of privacy about which the Canadian people have a right to know. Question No. 48 has been on the order paper for one year, or almost one year, dating from April 18, 1977. It concerns certain remarks which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made in a speech about a year ago. Finally, I refer to question No. 52 which was placed on the order paper last June, eight months ago, concerning Martin Goldfarb and the amount of public business he has received, he being the chief pollster for the Liberal Party of Canada.
I feel that if ten days is the limit, a member has a perfect right to rise, bring a question to the attention of the President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), and to ask him if he is prepared to guarantee that before this parliament is dissolved, whether it be this week, next week or the week after, as it surely will be, all questions on the order paper which have been there for more than four or five months will definitely be answered. I think it is a disgrace to every member who puts questions on the order paper that they are not answered and that the information requested is not forthcoming. I do not know how the minister can sit there, keep a straight face, look off into space, and have nothing to say on this subject. I hope he has the intestinal fortitude to rise at this time-not leave it to his parliamentary secretary-and tell us why, ten days being the rule, two years seem to be the actual fact.

speechtext:
I will deal with the question of parliamentary scrutiny of the operations of the pipeline agency in the course of my remarks.

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
It is not my intention to speak at any length at all because the issues involved in this legislation have been carefully considered by the standing committee, and yesterday the House of Commons dealt with all the amendments which had been put forward at the report stage of the bill.
The legislation governing the construction of a pipeline to carry both Canadian and United States natural gas from the Arctic to southern markets in both countries is necessarily lengthy and complex, but I am pleased to say that, despite very thorough and careful consideration by all members of the House, the main outlines of the bill and the framework of the legislation have emerged intact from that careful and thorough consideration.
At the same time the bill has been dealt with expeditiously, I believe reflecting a recognition of the immense contribution this project can make to the Canadian economy and to increasing our energy self-reliance. As hon. members recall, the bill was debated for seven days at second reading stage. The special committee which was established to consider the legislation in detail sat on 11 days and held 21 sessions. During that period it did receive the views of a substantial number of witnesses.
Certainly I would like to express my appreciation to members of the committee who attended with great dedication and who conducted the sessions with the minimum of partisanship and a maximum amount of cooperation. Also, I should like to express my appreciation to witnesses who appeared before the committee and whose views were carefully considered by members of the committee and, in some cases, whose views were directly reflected in amendments that were made to the bill either in the special committee or at the report stage of the bill itself.
A number of proposals were made in the committee, notably by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and other members, to improve and strengthen the bill. They were adopted unanimously. In fact it is worth mentioning that in the course of the committee's deliberations there was not a single recorded division. Every clause, every item before the committee, was accepted unanimously without any recorded division. But, of course, not included among the amendments that were accepted in the committee, or indeed at the report stage, is the matter of providing parliament with a continuing opportunity to maintain surveillance over the process of the project itself. I gave an undertaking in the course of the committee hearings that I would propose, on behalf of the government, an amendment to the standing orders establishing a continuing committee on northern pipelines. Hon. members will have noticed that there is on today's notice paper a motion in my name, proposing:
That Standing Order 65(1) be amended by adding immediately after subsection (s) the following:
"(t) Northern pipelines, to consist of not more than 15 members, to which shall stand permanently referred all reports, orders, agreements, regulations, directions and approvals mentioned in sections 12, 13, 14, 15 and 22 of the 
Northern Pipeline Act; provided that the said committee shall report thereon
at least three times in every sesssion."
Provided that this subsection shall be deleted from the standing orders on the day on which the Northern Pipeline Agency ceases to exist.
I propose, in reply to the questions raised by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), to call this motion and put it before the House as soon as it is appropriate to do so following the passage of the bill. I am not quite sure whether we must wait until the bill has received Royal Assent because of the reference to the sections of the Northern Pipeline Act, but in any event it is my intention to call the motion and have it adopted, if the House so wishes, at the earliest appropriate opportunity.
The creation of this special committee will make it possible for members of the House of Commons to sit with a continuing reference, and to receive reports, orders, agreements, regulations, directions and approvals as mentioned in the relevant sections of the bill. The committee, of course, will be free to organize its own activities, but this material will be automatically referred, and to ensure that the House will have an opportunity to examine the work of the committee there is a provision that the said committee shall report thereon at least three times in every session. I believe that is a reasonable stipulation which will provide the committee with occasions to meet and to report to the House. I believe that is a constructive provision.
From the very beginning I undertook in the House to ensure that parliament was brought in at every stage, and indeed we did provide for a debate in the House of Commons during last summer when all political parties had an opportunity to express themselves on the Berger inquiry and to indicate what, in their view, should be the main lines of any ultimate pipeline construction in Canada.
I am happy to say that the agreement which was negotiated between Canada and the United States and the bill which is now before the House contain, if not all, a substantial proportion of the suggestions and ideas that were put forward by members of all parties. Even though the New Democratic Party has raised certain objections to certain aspects of the bill, if reference is made to the speeches made on the occasion last summer and the philosophy outlined in those speeches, it will be found that a substantial part of the proposals made by them was reflected subsequently in the agreement and in the legislation.
In the case of the official opposition, I want to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Yukon and his colleagues on the committee for the constructive approach taken with a view to providing an expeditious passage of the bill, and also to providing certain changes which, in my view, were an improvement on the original measure as it was introduced in the House of Commons.
The last time I had the opportunity to put a major bill through the House of Commons was, of course, when I introduced the bill on the reform to the Election Expenses Act, and that, as hon. members will recall, was a major change in our electioneering. It will be applied, of course, for the first
April 4, 1978

time in the next election. However, political parties have already felt the benefits of that legislation, and political parties and candidates will appreciate even more the benefits that have accrued from the major undertaking. On that occasion as well there was a high degree of cooperation in the committee, and when the bill was passed it was, in a sense, a bill that had emerged from the House of Commons rather than the government itself.
I do not say that the same degree of consensus exists with respect to the northern pipeline bill, but I will say that, as time goes on, members as well as citizens throughout the country will appreciate even more the substantial benefits that will accrue to Canada in terms of increased production, employment, and access to energy reserves from the building of this huge pipeline system. The debate itself and the discussions in committee served to underline the enormity and the significance of these benefits.
Of course the question of Canadian participation and Canadian content has been a matter of debate. We dealt with amendments proposed on that subject yesterday. It is not my intention to relive that debate, except to say that evidence in committee, given by the company particularly and by officials from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, has certainly served to strengthen my conviction that Canadians will participate to the maximum possible extent in the construction of this line, and that the estimates which have been made by myself, when the agreement was signed and in the course of the debate, with respect to Canadian employment, Canadian jobs, impact on Canadian industry, and the benefits to Canada's balance of payments, will be fully realized.
In addition to what I have said already, it is important to underline the acute awareness on the part of hon. members on all sides of the House that this project be carried out in a manner which will minimize the adverse social and economic effects of the project on all of the people of the north, including the native people; and minimize the adverse effects on the environment in which they live and work, at the same time as ensuring that they will derive the greatest possible benefits both in the short run and over the longer term. We believe the project will contribute significant benefits to all of Canada, but we want to ensure that the adverse environmental and social effects be minimized. That sentiment was reflected in the comments made by all hon. members of parliament. I think that can be achieved, and I think the benefits for the northern people can be maximized during the course of construction.
In conclusion, I thank hon. members for the manner in which they have approached this measure. I wish to express the hope that it can be dealt with at this stage of the debate in the same expeditious manner which has characterized the preceding stages of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the remarks of the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) with interest, just as I listened with interest to his statements in response to questions put in the pipeline committee on which I was privileged to serve. That committee dealt with the entire aspect and many issues surrounding the Alaska pipeline.
In the area of another responsibility, which I share with other hon. members of the House, I have had some concern over the failure of one particular department to engage in any fashion in the discussion and debate surrounding the Alaska pipeline. That concern was reflected in Hansard dated March 16, 1978, when I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) about his role and his department's role in the development of the Alaska pipeline. By way of questions raised by the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), we had an opportunity to review the summary provided by DREE. It was a summary provided for the pipeline committee. I am not referring to the pipeline committee of the House, but rather of the government. Certainly the review occasioned some concern in the House which was demonstrated during question period. It concerned the degree of Canadian involvement in the project. Some of those concerns have been answered, and some will not be answered until the pipeline project goes forward.
The concerns which have not been answered with reference to the role of DREE appear to indicate on the surface that this is where the role of DREE will stop, rather than where the role of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will begin. In response to my question about his role, the minister provided me with vague and general rhetoric, without any categorical statement or indication that his department would be most substantially involved in the pipeline. The minister indicated that there had been some discussion with the province of British Columbia. He said that there had been no discussions with the municipalities, which is not quite correct. DREE officials have met with representatives of the regional district in a conference which was held in Fort St. John, a conference which was quite noticeable by the absence of any provincial representation. I see no reason why, in concert with provincial representatives, officials from the minister's department could not meet with municipal officials concerning the industrial infrastructure which is bound to follow the development of the pipeline, and perhaps even precede it.
The minister apparently thinks the service industries will have to respond. He said the same to me when I raised the question before the Standing Committee on Regional Development on March 21. At that time the minister said the following:
What we intend to do is to make sure that while the pipeline is being built we maximize the benefit to Canada and also, in your case, you were mentioning obviously British Columbia.
Also in response to my question in the House, he indicated that the service sector would certainly be involved. He said the following:

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
I think the service industries will have to respond to the opportunities that will be offered to them on the construction -
This gives me further cause for concern, because apparently no study is going forward or being planned for some semblance of orderly development of the service sector. Hopefully the service sectors will remain in an organized fashion in industrial parks or as needed. Certainly I hope we do not see the service sectors scattered along the route of the Alaska highway and the Alaska pipeline, eventually to become little isolated ghettos of rubbish and garbage which are so apparent after major construction projects of this kind. The minister has failed to address himself to this particular issue.
In response to my inquiry before the standing committee, the minister said that he intended to make sure there would be maximum benefits. He then went on to say the following:
-how to ensure the maximum benefit for B.C. in that instance through the whole exercise, I have no explicit plan in mind, but we have discussed that.
On the one hand the minister provided a statement through his departmental officials. A very substantial degree of analytical study went into that statement. The minister has indicated his department's concern only with reference to the future possibility of Canadian participation in the pipeline and the economic impacts. I must say I do not believe that particular aspect is in his mandate. Beyond that, when we move into the area of the minister's mandate dealing with economic development, the expansion of the economy, and areas which are disadvantaged, we find the minister really is not interested.
This morning, sir, before the same Standing Committee on Regional Development, I had an opportunity to ask the minister again whether he had expressed any concern to his provincial counterparts regarding the inquiry into the British Columbia railway. The minister apparently realizes, and his report indicates it, that rail is going to be one of the very substantial modes of moving pipe and other equipment to construction sites-at least in so far as rail runs into northern British Columbia. The minister's officials are not really aware of the fact that British Columbia had a very substantial inquiry into B.C. Rail. He is not aware that there has to be a very substantial upgrading of the roadbed before that rail system can provide the kind of service that is expected.
The minister has signed a subagreement as well with the province of British Columbia dealing with roads to resources in the north, whether they be railroads or highways, particularly in regard to coal development in the north. He did not seem to be aware this morning that, in fact, coal development in the north has been shunted aside because of the economy and the fact that coal is not selling. That particular type of soft coal has no market at this time.
The minister does not seem to be concerned over the fact that the forest industry, which is an important industry in northern British Columbia, also utilizes B.C. Rail and should also be receiving some form of assistance through DREE. He was unaware of the fact that the lieutenant governor of the

province, in delivering the throne speech a week ago, stated that the government was seriously concerned about the condition of the forest industry in the province.
You may ask, Mr. Speaker, what the forest industry in British Columbia has got to do with the pipeline. The simple fact remains that the subagreement with respect to northern British Columbia, where 500 miles of this pipeline will be built, has two subagreements dealing with transportation and with forest and coal development. It would naturally follow, in a government with any sense of organization and forward thinking, that if the economy of the north is to be developed in one way, whether it is coal or forest or pipeline, then one should complement the other. There should be a realization that there is, indeed, going to be a very heavy demand on those transportation modes. It should also be realized that the service sector alone is not sufficient in the way of DREE examination.
I am not suggesting to the minister or the government that there should be DREE funding for the service sector, Mr. Speaker. I think, sir, as most supporters of free enterprise would think, they should be able to fend for themselves. Surely DREE, in concert with its provincial counterpart, should be looking at the fact that the service sector is going to go forward. Further, the minister and his departmental officials should be reading what has been said in the pipeline debate about the type of industry which will go along with the construction of the pipeline and follow the eventual development of the line once the system is in operation.
The minister has given no indication whatsoever of any concern in this regard. Indeed, I would think that it would be the minister's responsibility to look at the type of equipment that is going to be used in this pipeline, and to think in terms of heavy equipment, which we traditionally import from the United States. He should reflect on the fact that heavy equipment, manufactured in Canada by Canadians for Canadians on the Alaska pipeline, may be a very sensible investment.
There is not only the Alaska pipeline. Surely, to follow, will be the Dempster lateral, and then some years down the line we will eventually see a polar gas route. Bearing this in mind, Mr. Speaker, the horizons that are there now and that are going to develop in the north, it would be wise for the minister to expand his thinking to include the north. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has failed in appreciating and seizing upon an opportunity to advance the economic development of this country. I am not surprised when I see the type of attention he has failed to give to probably the single largest opportunity that has ever slipped through that minister's grasp.
Again, 1 must state for the record that I am astounded at the generalizations made by the minister in response to questions that I have raised in the House and before the committee with reference to the Alaska pipeline. I am appalled at the failure of the minister even to address himself to this vital subject.
April 4, 1978

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the third reading stage debate on the bill on the northern pipeline. I want to reiterate the stand of the New Democratic Party in favour of the building of the northern gas pipeline, the Alcan pipeline as it is called.
Our concerns and, indeed, our reasons for voting against the bill that we have before us are that we feel it is inadequate and it does not represent the true interests of Canadians and Canadian companies. The bill has serious deficiencies and weaknesses, which I predict, some years down the road, will come back to haunt us. As I said, we are in favour of the Alcan pipeline running through Canada but we want to ensure that it will be built on the grounds that it will maximize Canadian content and Canadian jobs on the project. We have had assurances from the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mac-Eachen) that this will be the case. However, those verbal assurances for us are not enough. We want to see something written into legislation which will become the law of the land and will guarantee maximum Canadian content and Canadian labour participation in this huge undertaking. To that extent, we moved a number of amendments in the House of Commons yesterday which, regrettably, were voted down by both the Liberal and Conservative members.
It might be worth while, Mr. Speaker, to recall the position of the New Democratic Party when it became apparent that the Alcan pipeline would be chosen over the Canadian Arctic Gas submission to bring natural gas down through the Mackenzie Valley to the southern part of Canada, and to the United States. In the debate in this House of Commons on August 4, 1977, the leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), moved an amendment to the government motion recommending the Alcan pipeline route. His position in that amendment, is worth while recalling, and I would like to quote from page 8044 of Hansard:
-and after considering the evidence and reports of the relevant inquiries, this House approves the granting of a certificate for a pipeline through the southern Yukon as recommended in principle by the National Energy Board and the Lysyk and Hill inquiries, with particular reference to the following conditions:
(1)	That an Alcan pipeline authority be established immediately comprised of representatives of the native communities, labour, small business, consumers and conservationists from the affected pipeline corridor and from the federal, provincial and territorial governments, and that this authority be empowered to manage the regional impact of pipeline construction especially with respect to employment practices, and food, housing and utility prices as well as assuming the other responsibilities recommended by the above inquiries;
(2)	That a "Canada first" priority be enforced in hiring, contracting and supplying the pipeline with particular preference to local residents of the Yukon, British Columbia and Alberta in the vicinity of the pipeline route;
(3)	That no pipeline construction precede a fair settlement of the affected native land claims; and
(4)	That no pipeline construction commence before August 1981, and that the interval be used to inquire further into the local impact of pipeline construction, to determine final route selection, and to control project planning;
Northern Pipeline
and furthermore that exports of Canadian natural gas licensed for delivery to the United States after 1985 be considered as credits to be redeemed from the United States on an equivalent BTU basis."
Those were the conditions the NDP put forward and which we wanted to see incorporated in this legislation before us. Unfortunately, only part of those conditions are in the legislation. Indeed, the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council said he believed most of the conditions the NDP had asked for were met. I have to disagree with him on that point. We do have a committee, not only a government committee which will be supervising the planning and construction of the pipeline, but also, of course, the House of Commons committee which will be monitoring these developments.
Every member in this House knows from past history the attitude of this government to northern development. Not always has it been in the interests of northerners, and often their interests are sacrificed for the expediency of those more powerful interest groups in southern Canada. We also know from experience that this government has had a very sad record in protecting northern environment and the rights of native people in the north. It was this government and its former ministers of Indian affairs and northern development who were all gung-ho on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline route. So I am a bit suspicious that any agency set up by this government, and under this government's control, will prove to be beneficial to Canadian interests, and especially to northern interests.
I am also worried that the parliamentary committee, set up to monitor the progress of this pipeline will be ineffective in the long run. Every member in the House of Commons knows that every House committee is dominated by Liberal members. If there is an embarrassment to the government in terms of any phase of the construction or development of that pipeline, we all know that any attempts by opposition members to move correcting motions or courses of action are outvoted. All that we can hope for as an opposition is to generate enough publicity to embarrass the government into taking some corrective action.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this government has long since become insensitive to publicity. One thinks only of the examples of the economic problems in this country, the serious representations that opposition members have made to correct the situation and how those representations have fallen on deaf ears.
For these reasons the bill before us needed strengthening and yet we do not have these corrective measures in it.
The real concern my colleagues have is the lack of specific guarantees in the legislation to maximize Canadian content and participation. It was for these reasons that we moved a number of amendments to incorporate in the bill before us some very specific, concrete and clear demands on the government and the pipeline companies so that we would have, as the Deputy Prime Minister assured us verbally, at least 90 per cent Canadian content in this vast undertaking, and that we would have at least 100,000 man-years of employment during the construction of this pipeline. It seemed to us that if the

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
government is so confident that this could be achieved, it would have no objection to having such provisions in the legislation so that we could rely on law rather than on some cabinet minister's assurance, a cabinet minister who might be here today and gone tomorrow.
Why have we moved such amendments? Why are we so concerned that we will not achieve this maximization of Canadian content? We are concerned for a number of reasons. First I would like to cite some of the government's own departmental studies which have given rise to our concern.
We know that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion undertook a study of the proposed pipeline. They did an exhaustive analysis and came up with the conclusion, and we have quoted it in this House, that, unless there were guarantees, we could be more likely assured of only 67 per cent Canadian content, not the 90 per cent the minister promised, and not 100,000 man-years of employment, but more realistically somewhere between 60,000 and 68,000 man-years of employment. Surely if a respected government agency has produced a study like, this we should have some cause for concern if they are saying themselves that we need guarantees, or because of market situations and unfair trade situations and the way the treaty has been written, we will not get the maximum Canadian participation.
We have also heard reports from our friends in the American government. This is an energy pipeline and it will mainly benefit the Americans. It will move Alaskan gas through a Canadian land corridor to the 48 states. The Americans have been telling their business, their industry, and their Congress that it is a most beneficial undertaking. They have set up a situation or an agreement whereby they expect to achieve their maximum in terms of content and labour participation. Indeed the Americans are so confident that they predict 97 per cent American content in the Alaska portion of this pipeline yet here we are quibbling or afraid to even guarantee 90 per cent.
I recall when the Deputy Prime Minister first made the announcement after the negotiations and it was something like 98 per cent Canadian content. Then this figure was reduced to 90 per cent. The Americans are confident that they will get at least 97 per cent of the work on their section of the pipeline and will be employing American labour. It would seem to me we should be assured that we get maximum on the Canadian portion of the line.
We know the Americans have more competitive advantages, many more than we have in Canada. They have skilled labour which has recently worked on the Alyeska pipeline. This labour will be pressuring to move into northern Canada to work on the line here. As I say, I have some worry about whether our monitoring agency will be able to exclude these personnel, especially under the terms of some of the contracts that may be granted. We know there is American pipeline equipment that was used on the Alaska pipeline which has been bought up by American contractors at discounted prices. They are ready to go, in terms of submitting bids to work on the Canadian section of the line.

We should be guided by the fact that the Alyeska pipeline in the state of Alaska was eventually constructed with Japanese steel. It was not an American company that won the contract. I fear that this pattern may be repeated for the contracts issued on the pipeline coming through Canada. We have this government's studies and these American projections, all of which lead us to worry about whether we will get the 90 per cent content promised to us by the Deputy Prime Minister.
If the Department of Regional Economic Expansion Study is not enough to convince hon. members that there indeed may be some difficulties, I refer them to another report issued by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce entitled "Canadian Industrial and Manpower Requirements and Content for Northern Gas Pipeline". I went through this report in detail yesterday during the course of moving my amendments. I would again like to quote a couple of relevant sections from that report which back up the contention of this party that, unless we have these guarantees, we are not going to get the maximum benefits from the pipeline project. I quote from the report by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce:
Given that American firms are very well placed to win contracts for the U.S.A. portions, they, as a result, are in a more favourable position to bid on contracts for the Canadian segment by being able to pass on to the pipeline contractor some portions of the savings to be achieved by combining the Canadian requirements with their existing production for the U.S.A. sections of the line.
Here again American industry, through the efficiencies and economies of scale in terms of their production capacity for the sections of the line that will run through American territory, will have a competitive advantage over Canadian firms. That is an admission by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. That same report worries about the state of our economy in terms of the degree of foreign ownership and the relationship between subsidiaries and parent companies as far as Canadian content in this undertaking is concerned.
I again quote from the report:
The danger that sales contracts of Canadian branch plants of foreign multinationals which exceeded their existing capacity would simply be transferred to the non-Canadian parent instead of to alternative Canadian suppliers. Similar problems could occur if the low cost offshore plants were to be used to fill a bid made and originally intended for the successful Canadian subsidiary.
There is a very real possibility that Canadian companies will not get any spillover if American or foreign subsidiaries are producing at their maximum capability. Instead, that business will be transferred to the parent company of a subsidiary. I again quote from the Industry, Trade and Commerce report:
Competition in world markets is intense and Canadian companies could be outbid by the pricing strategies of Japanese and European pipe producers. Projections by steel experts reflect a tough world competitive situation.
The pipeline treaty between Canada and the United States allows for open competitive bidding. It is not just a bidding situation between the United States and Canada. Japan, West Germany, Italy, or any other foreign country which has a steel industry will be able to bid on the contracts for this pipeline. Surely hon. members do not need to be reminded that, in a world of international competition, all kinds of devices and
April 4, 1978

strategies are used that in the end amount to unfair competition, submitting bids at a low cost, bids that no Canadian company can match because of the lack of subsidies and other kinds of incentives provided by countries such as Japan.
This has been demonstrated again and again. I think, for example, of the latest charge under the Anti-dumping Act against Japan, by Algoma Steel in my constituency, for dumping on the Canadian market. There are also examples of American steel companies. One example is a recent pipeline contract in Mexico. American companies deliberately underbid 20 per cent so that they would get the contract for the Mexican pipeline and thereby not have to reduce the operation of their steel mills.
There is a slack in the world steel economy in terms of productive capacity. The bidding will be very intense. Is anyone naive enough to believe that the steel industry of Japan, West Germany, Italy, or the United States under the DISC program, will not have special concessions and assistance in terms of taxation policies, transportation policies or grant policies to allow them to submit bids in an unfair way to the detriment of Canadian steel producers?
The Canadian steel industry is confident it can win the bulk of the contracts on a competitive basis. We must remember it is an assumption of a fair competitive basis. I am worried that with unfair competition and lack of commitment in terms of some kind of guarantee, in the face of unfair competition Canadian steel companies and construction companies will not get the contracts for this undertaking. That is why we moved amendments recently to ensure that in the legislation we would have these guarantees of 90 per cent content and so on.
The government argues we cannot have that kind of guarantee in the legislation because it would be against the GATT treaty, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. I reject that argument. This is a bilateral agreement, an energy cooperation agreement between Canada and the United States. It mainly falls outside the narrow provisions of the GATT treaty. Indeed, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in its analysis of the situation correctly pointed out there have been precedents in the past relating to pipeline construction in both countries, the Interprovincial and the Portland-Montreal pipeline, as well as the Trans-Canada gas pipeline, whereby preference has been given to the country through which the pipeline passed in terms of construction and general contracts.
We made a mistake in the treaty that was signed with the United States, allowing for international competitive bidding. I am confident, if we had the competitive bidding within Canada, that our industry could meet the requirements of that pipeline construction at a fair cost. It is my worry that without guarantees we will find ourselves at such a competitive disadvantage that we will not get the maximum of the contracts. Certainly we may get something like 50 or 60 per cent. However, in light of the fact that we are taking all the risks for this construction, it is unreasonable because we will not be receiving the benefits in terms of natural gas until some long-off future date if and when a Dempster lateral spur pipeline is built in the Mackenzie valley.
Northern Pipeline
I have no qualms about arguing there should be provision for maximum Canadian participation. I think the government is using the GATT argument as an excuse. The monitoring committee of the House of Commons, as I have said, while a welcome improvement to the bill, will be powerless to redress any major setback in terms of Canadian content.
Mr. Speaker, another position taken by the NDP was that there should be no construction of the pipeline through the affected areas until native land claims had been settled. That amendment was not accepted by the House. We have offered another amendment which, in my opinion, is weaker but which, nevertheless, is better than nothing. It would provide that the native people's land claims would not be prejudiced while the pipeline continues to be built, supposing, of course, that they were not settled prior to the actual construction. My fear is that unless these land claims are settled before the pipeline construction commences, we shall be faced with a number of problems. I see real difficulty for Foothills in trying to raise the necessary capital in the financial markets of the world unless investors are assured that there will be no challenges in the courts by the native people, long litigation or other such delays in construction which will raise the cost of the pipeline. The only alternative, it seems to me, is to ensure the land claims issue is settled prior to the beginning of construction. Construction is not due to begin until 1981.
I had hoped that our amendment on the native claims issue would have brought pressure on the government to move expeditiously and fairly in getting a settlement to the land claims. We know the history of this government has been a sad one as it relates to the native people in terms of betrayal of their trust and interests. Had the amendment been passed it would have been a legislative incentive, an inducement to the government to stop dragging its feet and to get the land claims settled in a fair and judicious manner. Unfortunately, that amendment was not accepted. I hope the land claims issue, which unfortunately is now in limbo, but which could conceivably be a very contentious one if not settled by 1981, will not delay construction of the pipeline project, though, as I have said, I do have certain fears that it may do just that.
I am also puzzled in a way by some of the statements of my friends in the Conservative party who have rushed to the government's defence. I know the members who represent steel industry towns, such as the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), were very concerned, as we in the NDP were that the government did not see fit to legislate guarantees to maximize Canadian content and Canadian labour. Unfortunately, the minister has not been able to convince his colleagues that this represents a real danger and I regret his failure to do so.
Again, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has castigated the government for blaming the GATT agreement for its failure to include guarantees in the bill. That argument, too, seems to have been abandoned by his colleagues. I hope the Conservative party has not misplaced its trust in this Liberal government. I find it strange, in light of

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
the criticisms it has made of the way in which the goverment has behaved that the Conservatives have been willing to accept a bill which is in a weak form when it could have been strengthened considerably. For those reasons I regret that they have not supported the amendments we advanced.
This is a great undertaking, Mr. Speaker. It will mean a cost of some $10 billion, and it may mean at least some temporary relief to the massive unemployment situation we are facing as a result of Liberal government mismanagement of our economy. I hope that Canadian workers and Canadian companies a few years from now, when the contracts have been let and construction is under way, will not be short-changed by a bill which this House has been content to pass in the form now before us, when it had the opportunity to strengthen it by way of amendment. I hope the pipeline project proceeds without undue delay, without jeopardy to the environment, and in the interests of Northern Canadians and, indeed, of our friends in the United States. My only regret is that though we had the opportunity to improve the bill in significant ways for the benefit of Canadians, this House did not see fit to accept the needed amendments. I can only say my reservations still stand. 1 hope I am proved wrong. But the whole purpose, the whole stance of this party was to get the majority benefits for Canadians whom I thought we were elected to serve.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened carefully this afternoon to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) in his wrap-up speech on third reading and there was one area that I think he should have addressed himself to this afternoon, that is, the position of the churches of Canada with respect to the pipeline. I hope that the Deputy Prime Minister will find it possible to take note of what I am about to say because I think the brief which was presented to the cabinet just before Easter on behalf of the five major churches in Canada was a significant one and needs to be responded to by the members of the government and, failing that, certainly by members of this House.
Throughout this long process, from the beginning of the Berger and Lysyk inquiries, through the debate and work of the special committee and in the House, we know there have been small groups representing the churches-one might call them social activist groups-which have been lobbying very strongly against this bill and against the pipeline, largely on the grounds that the native people of the north are going to be hurt.
It was my feeling, as this process went on, that the objections these groups were making on behalf of the churches were being noted and taken care of and that there were answers to them. To my surprise, a few days before Easter, not a small group but the main delegation from the Roman Catholic, United, Presbyterian, Lutheran and Anglican churches-what might be called the mainline Christian churches of Canada- presented a brief to the federal cabinet which had to do with the ecumenically arrived at position of the churches on the economic outlook in Canada.
Four major areas of concern were outlined in the brief which was presented to the cabinet. The first was northern development, the second was income distribution, the third was investment transfers, and the fourth was regional disparities. I do not propose at this moment to go into all the implications of the comments made by the church leaders of our country in this interesting brief. I will save that for another occasion, but I do not think we can let this bill pass at third reading without responding adequately to the more or less up-to-date comments of the church leaders, who continue in their opposition to the northern pipeline.
The inter-church brief opposing the pipeline deals with four points. The first has to do with native land claims. On this point the church brief says the following:
The Council of Yukon Indians has our support in their insistence that these matters be settled and implemented before construction begins.
Second, the church brief makes the point that the second stage inquiry should be proceeded with in order to guarantee social justice with regard to the pipeline. Third, the interchurch brief asks how the government can guarantee for Canadians maximum benefits, and so forth. Fourth, in view of public criticism since the pipeline agreement was signed, the inter-church brief asks how Canadians will be assured that Canadian public funds will never be spent on the pipeline.
As a basis for the questions raised by the church leaders in opposing the pipeline I would like to refer to one or two sentences in their brief to explain the philosophy on which they based their questions. The inter-church brief says that a new industrial strategy is needed in our country and that this conclusion has been arrived at as a result of the contention that the present model of industrial development tends excessively to be capital-intensive, highly technological, energyintensive, export-oriented, and foreign controlled. The church brief sums up as follows:
To sum up on this point, we continue to see in the present pipeline plans a bleak economic outlook for Canadians-whether they be northern residents whose way of life and livelihood will be drastically changed, or southern residents for whom the main outlook seems to be the risk of further staggering increases in public debt.
A response to what I have quoted is needed. I intend to vote for this bill at third reading because I believe that the pipeline is needed for all the reasons we have been through over these past months. I also believe that the philosophy being advanced on behalf of the churches today is a philosophy which can lead us into a no growth situation. I make that comment respectfully to the church leaders.
I have received representations that I should oppose the bill, but the philosophy laid down by the churches in opposing the pipeline is a philosophy which would bring about quite the reverse of what the church leaders intend. The church leaders are arguing in the name of social justice. I believe that to conclude that the pipeline must not be built for economic reasons or for social reasons or that it must not be built before native land claims are settled, would be injurious to all Canadians and that would lead us away from the opportunities

April 4, 1978

for social justice that the church leaders want and which, indeed, I want.
Those who argue against the pipeline do us a service, however, because they make us focus on a just settlement of native land claims, on the social danger of destroying the native way of life, on environmental hazards, on the displacement of capital away from other pressing needs in southern Canada, on the voracious energy demands of the industrial machine which dominates western society, and on the need for us to change our way of life from resource exploitation to a new concept of stewardship, thus opening the way to a more just system of sharing wealth in the global community. That is a submission which church leaders as well as many responsible social analysts in Canada today are putting before the government. That philosophy can be found throughout the brief presented by the church leaders, although 1 have cited only a portion of it. The evidence which has been accumulated so far makes us aware of our responsibilities.
I think that what the church leaders and the coalition of social activists have been talking about over the past few months-and I support this-are changed attitudes which are necessary in today's economic society. I believe, however, that a pipeline can help us produce a climate in which people will be more receptive to the need for the changes for which the church leaders are arguing. The debate engendered by the pipeline hearings has sharpened our awareness.
The principal objection to the pipeline found in the up-to-date brief of the church leaders is on the ground that native claims have not been settled. I wish to make reference to the amendment which was introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), which I seconded. It is an amendment which was arrived at through the negotiating skills of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who, I think, very diligently throughout this whole process took careful account of the economic and social implications of the pipeline, and who worked in such a way as to strengthen the bill-the Deputy Prime Minister paid just tribute to that this afternoon-so that the best results would be obtained by Canadians generally, specifically including native northerners.
The amendment to which I want to draw the attention of the House reads:
Notwithstanding this act, any native claim, right, title or interest that the native people of Canada may have had prior to the coming into force of this act in and to the land on which the pipeline will be situated continues to exist until a settlement in respect of any such claim, right, title or interest is effected.
That motion was presented to us at report stage as motion No. 6, and it is in opposition to motion No. 4 put forward by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), the effect of which is to hold up the pipeline until all native land claims are settled. In my judgment, and I think in the judgment of several others, the effect of that motion would have been to kill the pipeline, or to hold it up for such an indeterminate period of time as to jeopardize the success of the project and the commitments that were made by the Government of Canada,
Northern Pipeline
with the concurrence of parliament, that the pipeline should be started.
Therefore, I think that we should look now to the special parliamentary committee which will act as an ongoing parliamentary monitoring agency, in addition to the regulatory agency which has been established, to ensure that the economic and social benefits are intertwined in a just way. I believe that this can be done. I think that the optimism expressed by the government that a settlement will be reached is perhaps reflective of the optimism which the government always brings to a statement of justice on behalf of minority groups. Of course, the proof is in the pudding.
I think that we will only obtain that justice in native settlements, we will only obtain the justice that the church leaders want for northerners in the dislocation they will be undergoing, if the ongoing situation is very carefully monitored and if pressure is exerted on the government by members of parliament and members of the committee to ensure that the settlements affecting the way of life of the northerners are handled in such a way that the benefits of the construction- the largest construction project in the history of Canada- meet the needs of both the southerners and northerners combined.
1 think that if we ask ourselves whether we should halt the construction of the pipeline until the native land claims are settled, we should also ask ourselves whether we are not jeopardizing our relations with the United States and antagonizing the non-native Yukoners, not to mention a significant portion of Canadian labour. I do not think that that is a solution, which is why I personally oppose motion No. 4 and support the motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. I think that pressure must continue to be exerted on the federal government to achieve a just settlement, and in the next three years the federal government must work just as diligently toward the achievement and implementation of a settlement as it will be working toward the construction and operation of the pipeline.
In the continuing examination of this project by the two groups I have mentioned, I would anticipate and urge that we see some concrete proposals on what the federal government intends to do about the Indian land claims. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENSURE LEGIBILITY OF DOCUMENTS RECEIVED BY SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
that Bill C-208, an act to render government documents and publications pertaining to senior citizens more legible and comprehensible, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
Document Legibility
He said: In my experience as an MP I think one of the most satisfying and rewarding aspects of this job is the opportunity that we have as members of this institution to become associated with groups of retired Canadians, the senior citizens of this country, who have formed themselves into a wide variety of New Horizons Clubs and other types of senior citizens' organizations in all parts of Canada.
I am sure, as all other hon. members do, I welcome those occasions when I have the opportunity to visit these clubs and groups and meet with their membership. The time spent is very worthwhile because it is rare that one will find the depth of knowledge and the wealth of experience assembled together in one place that you will encounter in the drop-in centres and other meeting places created by the New Horizons programs of the Government of Canada, and in the clubs and organizations of senior citizens across the country created by other public and private programs.
For any member of parliament or any other interested person, the analysis of issues to be found in these places and the ideas which are put forward, whether those issues are large or small, local, provincial, regional, national or international, are very much worth listening to and heeding with care.
In Assiniboia constituency I am pleased to say we have more than 50 active projects operating under the auspices of the New Horizons program. Our part of southern Saskatchewan is fortunate to have a number of other agencies and organizations of particular relevance to older people. The idea for the proposal contained in Bill C-208 now before us in fact originated in the discussions which I have had from time to time with the members of these various clubs, agencies, and groups in the Assiniboia constituency. I am sure my experience in this regard has been duplicated many times over in virtually all parts of the country.
In proposing this bill, Mr. Speaker, I want to pay a special tribute to Mrs. Ivol Krueger and to all of those who have been involved in such a dedicated way on the New Horizons committee of Weyburn, Saskatchewan, and the very active "Aid for the Aging" group in that community. Their efforts in drawing attention to the particular issue dealt with in Bill C-208, and their work on behalf of senior citizens in so many other ways, is a prime example of spirited and effective community service. I hope that this House can add to those efforts in some small way by adopting this bill, or at least by adopting the idea in principle and allowing the matter to go to a House committee for detailed analysis and consideration.
The gist of Bill C-208 is captioned quite well in its short title "An Act to render government documents and publications pertaining to senior citizens more legible and comprehensible". It is brief, as hon. members can see, consisting basically of three short clauses. The major provisions are really two in number. First of all there is a requirement through this bill that the Queen's Printer print all publications specifically intended for senior citizens in a large and clear style of type. Secondly there is a provision which would require the Queen's Printer to make specific documents available on request to

April 4, 1978
Document Legibility
senior citizens if they have a particular need for them. These documents should be printed in a large style of type in order that these people can make use of them.
There are two additional clauses in the bill. One would authorize the minister to make the appropriate regulations to implement the thrust of the legislation. The other is a short definition clause defining precisely that "senior citizen" refers to people who have reached the age of 65.
I am sure that rationale behind this kind of proposal is perfectly obvious and will be well understood by hon. mem-oers. As people get older, eyesight often tends to fail. Therefore, regular sized print or type used in official publications is often not adequate to meet the physical requirements of senior citizens.
In my office today I received an orange booklet put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare. It is entitled "Basic Facts of Social Security Programs". It is a very useful booklet, and it contains approximately 45 pages. In this booklet there is information about various programs and activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Unfortunately every page is chock-full of very small, fine print. It is extremely difficult to be able to read such a document in an easy way and to comprehend what is being said in that document, even with perfect eyesight. I am sure that to anyone who has any impairment of vision this document might be almost unreadable not because of what is contained in it, but because of the style, type, and method of printing used.
As older people struggle to deal with the papers they have to read and cope with, they are subject to a considerable amount of unnecessary strain, physical eye strain as well as emotional stress or strain. Sometimes of necessity, because there may be no alternative, documents like that one and even others of greater importance simply get ignored.
In discussing this issue with senior citizens themselves, another interesting point was brought to mind. In days gone by, many people who are now in the older age bracket did not have access in their youth to the formal educational facilities available in Canada today. As a consequence they are often apprehensive or even frightened to tackle government documents, forms and publications. It is ironic, and I think unfortunate, that these people, who are often so properly referred to as the "salt of the earth" or the "backbone of the country", are sometimes intimidated by some of the complexities and the complications placed on them by the country to the building of which they have contributed so much. Sometimes it seems to me that this intimidation or that feeling of inadequacy can have very serious consequences, Mr. Speaker.
I am told by senior citizens that a prime case in point is in relation to the various federal-provincial old age income supplement plans for which senior citizens must make application. These plans are not available to senior citizens automatically when they reach a certain age. They must apply to the various departments responsible for the administration of the programs in order to entitle themselves to benefits.

Specifically, I think of the guaranteed income supplement program. This is a program which is very useful to senior citizens on limited incomes. But the important fact to remember is that this program is not automatically available to senior citizens upon their attaining a certain age. They must file an application for it. In order to know that they must do that, they have to be able to read documents like this one, to which I have just referred. This document outlines the details of that particular program and makes it clear that an application must be filed. In addition to that they must be able to deal with the application itself in a reasonable way, to read it, to understand it, and to file it, in order to entitle themselves to those benefits. If the form or the book itself is not printed in a way that is easily read, then that, of course, impedes the making of that application. That is a rather serious consequence which should be a relatively easy problem to solve.
Income tax forms are another problem. Those closely associated with programs involving older people can attest to the fact that every year at tax time some senior citizens actually become physically ill in having to contend with the complex and finely printed documents and forms which come to them during the time when income tax documentation must be completed. I suppose there is no formal documented evidence on this point. But I am content to rely upon the observations of those who have been very active in helping to serve senior citizens. Again I refer to Mrs. Krueger of Wey-burn, and many others like her, who can speak from years of observation in actual experience in this field. They know the kind of anxiety that senior citizens experience when confronted with difficulties of this kind.
The problem could be alleviated in some small part by ensuring that the relevant printed material is in fact printed in a manner which can be easily read. That would be a step in the right direction. It would help to reduce some of the uneasiness and frustration which some senior citizens presently experience when trying to grapple with the documentation with which they now have to deal.
The idea contained in Bill C-208 is obviously not a cure-all for all of the difficulties with which older people must deal in encountering government agencies and other institutions, both public and private. The complexity of life in this day and age is unfortunately more than any of us would like to see. At least this bill would implement one measure which might be of positive, practical assistance.
I do not pretend that this is a perfect proposal in Bill C-208. It has some obvious defects. For example, it is specifically tied to the needs of older people. There are many Canadians under the age of 65 who also suffer from impaired vision. Conversely, there are a great many senior citizens who enjoy perfectly good eyesight and might not require the large style of type proposed in this bill. Nevertheless, this is an important matter for the House to consider. I appreciate the attention hon. members are giving to it this afternoon.
April 4, 1978

If there is general agreement that the subject matter of this bill is worthy of further examination but the specifics proposed in it are not precisely appropriate, I would have no objection to the motion being amended to refer the subject matter only to the appropriate committee to consider and study a matter of this kind. It might not be the Miscellaneous Estimates committee. It might well be the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. If it were the disposition of the House to make that amendment and refer the subject matter, I would be happy to see the matter go forward in that way. In that forum, such as a committee of this House, we could more thoroughly canvass this whole area of concern and identify the best technical way to solve what is a very real problem for older people and for certain other Canadians as well.

Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate on a very interesting and worth-while topic, I commend the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) for bringing to the attention of the House concerns of senior citizens. As I read the wording in the bill, as a legislator I have some reservations as to just what we might be legislating by bringing this specific bill into force or into committee for possible amendment, as the hon. member suggested. Bill C-208 is, and I quote:
An Act to render government documents and publications pertaining to senior citizens more legible and comprehensible
If we were to pass this bill, we would be amending the Department of Supply and Services Act to require, and I quote:
The Queen's Printer for Canada shall
(a)	print any publication that is distributed to senior citizens pursuant to the
Old Age Security Act or the Canada Pension Plan in large and clear type, and
(b)	provide on the request of any senior citizen a copy in large and clear type
of any publication that is printed on behalf of any department or agency of the
Government of Canada.
(2)	The Minister may make regulations respecting the printing and distribution of publications for carrying out the purposes outlined in subsection (1).
(3)	In this section "senior citizen" means any person who has reached 65 years of age."
There are a number of concerns that will come out of the course of this discussion that will not in themselves take away from the point that is being made by my colleague from Assiniboia. But they perhaps give us some reservations in terms of putting this legislation on the books before we have a much deeper look at the substance.
Let us talk about the criteria. The bill refers to age. The hon. member for Assiniboia indicated that age might not be the only criterion. There might be other criteria that should be examined. I have many senior citizens' residences in my constituency. In them are people of various physical situation. If the criterion is age, we are setting an artificial barrier by putting in age 65. However, I am not sure this would be a valid criterion for inclusion in legislation of a more general nature of this sort. We would in effect be creating two classes of citizens at the taxpayers' expense, one privileged, and the other not. How do we readily identify citizens with a reading difficulty? If age is used, reaction from older persons past the chosen age limit or barrier who have no such problems will be critical. The problem relates primarily to the identification of the audience for each publication put out by the 128 departments and agencies of the Government of Canada. In addition to that general criteria problem, I would like to speak for a few moments on the matter of cost. It would be unfair for us as parliamentarians at this time to brush over this issue and see the bill go to committee before we have the benefit of discussion on what kind of costs might be involved in making an amendment of this nature to the Supply and Services Act.
It is going to be very difficult to assess the cost figure and the actions required to implement successfully what is called for in Bill C-208. That becomes obvious as we examine the details of the bill as I enunciated them earlier. If the likely cost cannot be calculated with some degree of accuracy, it would be imprudent on our part to adopt this amendment before endeavouring to assess just what it is to which we are exposing the Canadian taxpayer.
A costing of these responsibilities presupposes at least the ability to do a number of things. We must be able to identify which government publications should be printed in the larger type size, and why. I am sure that my colleague from Assiniboia would be the first to say it should not necessarily apply to all government documents, only when there seems to be a particular need. This again gets into the criteria question, which document should be and which should not.
We would need to have the ability to specify the required quantities of each identified publication in each official language. There are massive publications hour by hour, day by day, in the various government departments and agencies in the over-all government service. In each specific case, someone would have to pinpoint how many would need to be printed in the larger type and in both official languages. Would it be the same number in English and French, or more English and less
