French? What would be the percentage? How would that be established?
In addition, a method of distribution would have to be established. In other words, after these copies have been produced in large type in English and French, what do you do with them? Presumably they are distributed to someone. The question is, who gets them? Is it the intention to wait for applications to come in from Canadians who, perhaps, would have to be over a certain age in order to qualify to receive these publications in the larger type? How does one go about this process? The demand may, in the end, turn out to be very small. We could be piling up surpluses in printed paper, publications which may never be requested or, indeed, required. Just what are we getting into in terms of the inventory of these special issues?
Then there is the question of frequency. How often will these publications be brought out? Would every issue be treated in the way suggested, or only the more important ones? Where would a limitation be placed? What I am really saying is that the range of possibilities or options in layout and type size is really too broad to enable us to make any reliable estimate as to cost, and in these circumstances it would be somewhat irresponsible for us to allow the bill to become law.
There are, however, two basic factors which can be recognized immediately as likely to have an effect on costs. And each of them implies additional costs. The first is that in most cases a larger type face will put less characters on a page, thus requiring more pages or larger pages to achieve the same quality of communication. This means more paper, and, if there are to be more pages, additional sheets to be run through the printing presses. Already many of us are receiving criticism from our constituents about the amount of paper we generate in the system. And most of us here would agree there are times when we are ourselves overwhelmed by the quantity of paper which is churned out day after day for our attention.
The second factor is that the number of the older generations will increase over the years, implying an increased audience for such publications if they are based on the somewhat dubious criterion of age. In other words, the percentage of the population over the age of 65 is rising rather rapidly, so the demand might be expected to increase.
A further alternative, and one which has the virtue of eliminating doubtful selection criteria, would be to instruct the Queen's Printer to produce all government publications and tracts in type of not less than a given size, thus assuring the reading comfort of any citizen suffering from a corresponding degree of restricted vision. Two problems immediately emerge, however. First, the cost of all government printing would automatically increase, although percentage increases would probably vary with different publications. In the second place, defining a corresponding degree of restricted vision which made any sense would still leave citizens, whose eyesight is more seriously impaired, without an increase in their reading

comfort. What is the correct reading impairment cut-off point?
These are just some of the problems to be faced. I am simply pointing out the need for a much closer examination of the criteria of which we are speaking if we are to take this legislation through the whole process and make it an official amendment to the Supply and Services Act. It is my view that as members of parliament we should be concerned about the cost we are imposing upon the taxpayers generally. If we were to pass this measure I assume there would be considerable pressure on provincial governments and municipal governments to take similar action. It is my observation that municipal governments, in particular, often make use of print sizes which are very small.

I suggest that the bill should be broader than that and our concern should relate to all Canadians so that they can deal at least with the government, if not with private agencies, by way of documents printed in a way that is readable to them. So Count von Bismarck said: "That is a good idea; that is exactly what we should do". He asked his adviser what age he would suggest, and the man said: "Sixty-five is the age when you should start to put people on compulsory retirement". So the chancellor said: "Why 65?" At that time the life expectancy of people in Germany was 55, so he figured very few of them would reach age 65. That is why the figure of 65 was agreed on.

A number of delays in conjunction with incomplete planning constituted the reason for massive over-runs on the Alaska project, which met with economic tragedy. We cannot afford such over-runs on this project.
One thing the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) and others of that party have failed to recognize is that this is a project which will not involve the expenditure of any taxpayers' dollars. It is a project which is being undertaken by the private sector entirely, and that should not be overlooked. In light of this critical delay factor and the importance to the nation of the project over-all we should have expected more leadership. I say that kindly in light of the very kind remarks of the Deputy Prime Minister with respect to myself in my committee activities.
There have been government shortcomings. They could have introduced this bill last fall. They could have given us more opportunity in committee to examine the project more thoroughly. They have not given the leadership which should have been expected but was not forthcoming. We were presented with a bill which was very deficient, and that is implicit in the remarks of the Deputy Prime Minister. It was drafted in a fashion which virtually eliminated the judicial review processes of the bill.
There was no mention of the native presence or any review process whatsoever to ensure the observance of the Canadian content provisions spelled out in the international agreement. Also, there was an absence of watchkeeping or safeguards to keep watch over the exercise of very wide discretions granted to the minister, to the agency and others having authority under the bill.
For a party that should have been displaying leadership on such an important issue to this country, they have failed to an extent that was a surprise to us. In retrospect, perhaps it was not such a surprise in view of the extent to which the government accepted the amendments which we proposed. For example, I have mentioned that proper planning and preparation, the avoidance of delays, which was absolutely critical to the success of the project, and the recognition of native rights should have been an integral part of the planning process. Instead, we have the native groups appearing before the
Northern Pipeline
Commons and Senate committees virtually unannounced in their indictment of the government's lack of planning of concern for these people. The government should have shown concern with singular focus on native rights, rather than on the over-all concern for the total population in the areas which would be traversed by the pipeline itself.
The most glaring omission-and even I was surprised at this because I thought that the government would have been more closely attuned to this factor-was the total failure to look into the native environmental situation in northern British Columbia. The Yukon at least had Lysyk and the promise of a second stage inquiry, which is now resolved by the government's acceptance of an amendment which will ensure that an advisory council will be set up for the Yukon. The NWT had Berger. But northern B.C. had nothing. It spite of the fact that more pipe will be running through B.C. than the Yukon, they were completely ignored. Anyone studying the matter will immediately come to the conclusion that the environment and the socioeconomic impact of the pipeline is just as important in northeastern B.C. as in the Yukon.
One cannot help but reflect on this government and its consultative practices. So much for the just society, so much for participatory democracy and so much for the consultative process. It simply results in bad management, and that is the bottom line. It is plain bad management. It is insensitivity as well as lack of foresight. How can you expect, for instance, the native organizations in British Columbia to react favourably when they are not even consulted? How, indeed, can you expect anyone else to co-operate with the government in a project of this size? Really, they jeopardized their own project. Indeed, the approach taken by the government party invites obstruction. It invites lawsuits and delays in construction.
The same thing happened to the Alyeska project. It resulted in huge over-runs, and I might add-and I hope this does not happen in Canada-that that line has been sabotaged twice deliberately. It is an inevitable implication in the climate of suspicion and resentment such as this that both this project and the national interest cannot help but suffer. Whatever delays occur-and they have occurred already-will be completely the fault of the government. It is their inability to manage and provide leadership for this massive undertaking of extremely strategic importance to Canada.
Our approach from the outset has been to expedite the passage of this bill. We have taken the leadership in making a bill out of a non-bill. Confronted by a seriously deficient piece of legislation, as was this bill, we had to optimize this tremendous opportunity to help the country out of its current malaise. It was we who initiated the discussions relating to changes which would recognize native concerns and formalize the judicial review provisions. It was we who initiated the discussion with respect to the plan of parliamentary review of the decisions and agreements and other matters involving the sections of the bill which are going to be the subject matter of the resolution proposed by the Deputy Prime Minister. We were the ones who devised the parliamentary plan of review,

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
which is the only acceptable alternative to ensure Canadian content.
We recognize that an explicit guarantee of Canadian content was impossible, for the reasons I have already expressed, namely that it offended the international agreement as well as the terms of GATT. We have accepted the assurances of the company that is going to be building the pipeline, and we have accepted the assurances of the Deputy Prime Minister and of the government that material and labour procurements will not be approved which do not optimize the Canadian content possibilities.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie overlooks the fact that the designated minister will have that power under the bill. That will undoubtedly be explained by the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who explicitly examined the minister when he appeared before the committee with respect to powers in that respect.
In addition, we added the provision for a parliamentary review of such approval by a standing committee. This is unique in my experience in this House, where the standing orders have been amended to provide for the establishment of a special committee for this specific purpose. Given these constraints, plus the fact that neither industry nor labour wants the kind of changes that the member for Sault Ste. Marie has been advocating, our approach is by far the most reasonable. It is the only acceptable approach.
We were the only party which proposed imposing a limit on the cost of the agency which could be passed on to the company. That proposal was made by the member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden). It was ruled out of order. This party thought that was essential. It is included in the American legislation but it is not in ours.
Our intention was not to pass on these costs to the people of Canada as taxpayers, but rather to impose a lid on the bureaucratic growth that we are all too familiar with respecting the unwieldy, unresponsive, secretive and expensive bureaucracies of this government. We thought a lid would impose a discipline which would keep those costs under control. The government argued against it and the proposal was ruled out of order. All of these measures we presented in committee. This was not done by the NDP. At the last moment they introduced amendments which they should have introduced in committee. We think that lid was important. We think that lid would have enhanced the position of the companies in the debt financing markets, and that is precisely why the provision is in the American legislation.
It is my belief, and I say this kindly to the government, that the number and the scope of our amendments clearly show that this government still does not know what it is doing wrong. They plod on and they keep making the same mistakes over and over again. It was our party which also expressed concern over the possibility that a controlling interest in the project might fall into foreign hands. We obtained an amendment which places the responsibility upon the governor-in-

council, the cabinet, to approve any alteration in the shareholdings of the companies undertaking the project. That, we thought, was essential.
A final point remains which still causes some concern, and that is the absence of some assurance that Canadian gas will flow to Canadian consumers through this pipeline. This was one of the key points raised in debate last August-that we must maximize the potential benefits to Canadians that may issue from this project. At the time it was stated by our leader that it was imperative that the government and the Alcan proponents begin immediately environmental and other studies to tell us whether a Dempster connection was feasible. Today, almost eight full months later, there are not only no reports, but no studies have been initiated.
At committee we continually probed and questioned in an endeavour to find out whether Canadian gas would indeed flow through this line. We were continually assured it would, but assurances are all that the Canadian people have received. They have received no action in the way of setting up the machinery to prepare these reports. I believe that this point is critical. How are we to move to energy self-sufficiency? How are we to rectify our trade imbalances? This government is dragging its feet. When I speak of delays in introducing the bill, the delays apply equally to the absence of any action in exploring the Dempster lateral.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker; 1 can finish in just two minutes. The government is dragging its feet. That, coupled with the initial delays of the New Democratic Party, has delayed this bill. The NDP seems to have had a change of heart, perhaps because of pressures from the west. One can conjecture about that.
While the title of the act refers to a pipeline for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska and northern Canada, the definition of "pipeline" is, and I quote, "the pipeline for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska across Canada along the route set out in Annex I". This route does not include the Dempster or any other route to Canadian sources, and that to my mind is not good management. It is not leadership. I think they could be missing their big chance. The government is not maximizing this opportunity. The government has delayed the bill. It should have been introduced last fall. We had urged that last August through our leader. They have not used the intervening time to study that route.
The position of the NDP is simply not acceptable. They voted against the bill at second reading. What will they do at third reading? That is left to conjecture. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands accepted every one of our amendments in committee. He did not introduce any from his own party. Amendments should be discussed in committee
April 4, 1978

where witnesses are available and where we can have free discussion and cross-examination of witnesses.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was absent, I am sure for a legitimate reason, when the matter came on at the report stage and the responsibility was left to the hon. member for Sault Ste Marie. His presentation displayed an absolutely abysmal ignorance of what went on in committee. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was concerned about two things. He was concerned first of all about Canadian content, and he was concerned secondly about native rights. He listened to me, as I did to him in committee. The Canadian content and those guarantees are adequately protected by the acceptance of the government of our suggestions for parliamentary review, which is where it should be and nowhere else, and because it is impossible in the legislation itself.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands does not understand the situation with respect to the residents of the Yukon as a whole, and the native people there in particular. While the native people say that I do not represent their interests in this forum, what they really mean is that I do not agree with their views. I do not, and this party does not. It does not stand to reason that any development should be impeded or stalled or held up if the negotiating process is still a reasonable process to follow. Without the one prejudicing the other, there is no reason in the world why those negotiations cannot result in a just and fair settlement of the native claims, with development taking place at the same time. Logically, if you adopt any other conclusion there will be no road built, no bridge built and no new mine brought into production. Everything is stalled until the native demands are met, if they are to be met. That is an intolerable position, in a project of such national interest as this, for the New Democratic Party to be taking.
I chastise the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, although I would like to be as fit as he when I reach his age to enforce that chastisement-which I would probably be unable to do successfully even with our age difference now-for not introducing amendments at the committee stage. I chastise him and his party for agreeing with every amendment that we advanced at the committee stage and then at the report stage coming up with the ill-advised and empty amendments which he proposed.
When they charge us with defending the government's position, they are twisting the truth. The government came in with a weak bill. It is through our amendments that the bill is now at least half acceptable. There are still weakneses, but we negotiated for as much as we could get. I suggest to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that in the national interest his party is compelled to vote for the project.
They have the guarantees that they wish through the overview of the parliamentary committee. That should satisfy him and his colleagues. They have the judicial provisions completely revamped so that there is no impediment to freedom of
Northern Pipeline
access to the courts by the individual. That was not in the original bill. It is there because of us. Clause 16, with its broad, sweeping powers, is wiped out because of our objections. That should satisfy them. All of the other major amendments which we proposed in committee have been accepted by the government.
If the gloomy predictions of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie occur and if the control or ownership of the mine passes from Canadian hands, it will be on the head of the government, not on the head or in the discretion of a single minister, because of our proposals.
Something I want to emphasize is that the amended bill as it came back from committee was a result of the amendments of this party only. There was no input whatsoever in the way of amendments from the New Democratic Party. That I chastise them for. If they were really sincere and if there were no hypocrisy about their position, that is where their amendments should have been brought in.
The government has to be chastised for their delay, not because of the presentation of the project in the national interest. Through no fault of the Deputy Prime Minister- because he was ill-it was not treated with very much importance in the two days before we recessed for Easter. The first day it was left to a minister who knew nothing of the terms of the agreement itself. The second day it was left to my friend and colleague, whose constituency I cannot identify at the moment, but who also is not a member of the committee.
It seems rather a shame that they would treat in such cavalier fashion a bill of this importance. The magnitude of the project, the importance that it has to Canada as a whole, the bottom line being the creation of a new industry which has the potential of bidding competitively and successfully throughout the world in a pipeline industry, cannot be overlooked. For those people on the left to adopt stalling and delaying tactics, voting against it on second reading-and who knows what they are going to do on third reading-is very patently against the national interest. In my submission, that is what we must be concerned with here.
The government could have handled this project much better than it did. It could have negotiated a much better agreement, particularly with regard to my constituency, something I will take up elsewhere. However, for anyone in this House to vote against this project in my submission, and in the submission of this party, is sheer irresponsibility, because it leaves too much at this critical stage of our, to put it kindly, extremely disturbed economy.

Our objections to this legislation lie basically in two areas. First, there is the agreement itself which the bill before us virtually ratifies. We think the agreement was ill-conceived and hastily considered. We believe the government entered into an under-

standing which is not in the national interest. In the second place, we are critical of the legislation not so much for what it contains in its amended version as for what is omitted.
Members have criticized me for not moving any amendments in committee. Well, first of all, the Conservative members moved some good amendments which I supported. As for the amendments which were proposed by the Council of Yukon Indians, by the Committee on Arctic Research and by the Committee for an Independent Canada, I asked both the government members and the opposition members if they were prepared to support them. They were turned down. It would have been of no use at all to go through the charade of one member of the committee moving proposals which it was perfectly clear neither the government members nor the opposition members would support.
1 agree that the bill was greatly improved in committee. Many of the most obvious deficiencies were removed and I commend the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) for adopting the changes proposed. To have really amended the legislation would have required redrafting the bill. It would have required amendments which no private member could have introduced.
I suppose we could now, at third reading, move a motion to refer the bill back and ask the government to negotiate with the United States so as to make fundamental changes in the legislation. But that would simply be histrionics. The government has been pushing this bill through as quickly as it can- too quickly, in my view, to allow for proper and careful consideration to be given to it. There is no doubt that the official opposition is gung-ho when it comes to getting this measure through, as the hon. member for Yukon has demonstrated again and again. The fact remains, though, that this House is about to take part in putting on the statute books a piece of legislation in which there are glaring gaps and deficiencies, shortcomings which will become more obvious as the project proceeds.
Let me remind hon. members that we are passing this legislation despite the fact that there has so far been no agreement with Foothills, the company which was recommended by the National Energy Board to get a certificate of public convenience. This is the company which is to be allowed to proceed with the project. The agreement is presently being negotiated. We do not know what it is to contain, yet the agreement is important for a number of reasons. For example, it will set forth the hiring procedures and the timetable for construction of the project. Most important of all, it will set forth the environmental impact protection provisions.
I do not think sufficient consideration has been given to environmental protection. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), quoting this afternoon from a brief submitted by the churches of Canada, made the comment that he thought the position they were taking really amounted to a philosophy of no growth. Mr. Speaker, I have read that brief. I do not agree with him, but I don't think it envisages a no growth situation. What it does, though, is remind parliament and the government that it should be possible to get economic
April 4, 1978

growth without destroying the environment; that it should be possible to improve the living standards of this generation without destroying the prospects of the next generation living well. Surely those two things are not mutually exclusive.
I believe there has been a complete failure to understand the dangers which are implicit in this project. We might have been in a position to assess what the government had in mind if we could have examined the agreement with Foothills Limited. But we do not have that document. We have the report of the Lysyk inquiry which took only three months. Dean Lysyk himself, at every hearing, told those who came: This is only a preliminary inquiry; there is to be a second review. In point of fact, there will be no second inquiry. Committees will be set up and so on, but most of the plans will already be under way by then. There is a serious failure to put anything concrete in the legislation along the line that we want the pipeline but we do not want the environment of northern Canada destroyed or the livelihood of its people impaired.
Further, the United States government has not yet set a price for the gas, and in consequence Foothills Limited has not been able to get any gas contracts. And because it has not been able to get contracts, it cannot arrange any of its financing. No financial institution is going to buy bonds or debentures from a company which has not signed any firm contracts.
Again, there is nothing in the legislation about cost over-runs.

Thirdly, there is no agreement which has yet been reached with the native people who will be affected by this pipeline. Negotiations started with the Council of Yukon Indians as far back as 1973. On February 14 of this year the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) said he hoped we were making progress but, of course, we hoped we would make progress and have a settlement in principle last fall. Now we are hoping we might have it soon. But there is still no settlement at all, and if we do not move any more quickly in the next four or five years than we have moved in the last four or five years, there will not be any settlement prior to the commencement of construction of this pipeline.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) was quoted by the media a few months ago as saying he could not agree that there should be no commencement of construction until a settlement had been reached, because that would allow the native people to hold the country up to blackmail. The hon. member for Yukon reiterated the argument again this evening that we cannot allow one small group of people to hold the nation up for ranson. He went so far as to say that even if the whole of his area were against this legislation he would support it because it is in the national interest.
On the other hand, surely any minority group in this country has a right to consideration, and what we are doing when we pass this legislation is putting the shoe on the other foot. What we are saying with this legislation is that we are going to build the pipeline. We are telling the native people that they had better sign the agreement we have put in front of them or the project will begin, and once the project is finished the chances of getting a settlement are extremely remote.

speechtext:
Of course it is after the fact, and the hon. member knows that, but he wants to pretend he does not. Surely hon. members of this House who have listened to briefs presented by native people, not only from northern Canada but also from southern parts of Canada, know perfectly well that probably the blackest page in the history of this country is our treatment of native people. We robbed them of their land, we deceived them and we made promises to them which we have not kept.
Most native people in Canada live in dire poverty, stuck on reservations, and some of them not even on reservations. They

have no agreement and no treaty. Our forefathers might have been excused. I personally do not excuse them, but they might have been excused by virtue of the fact that they did not realize the enormity of the crime which was being perpetrated. However, we in this parliament cannot claim ignorance. We know what has happened, and we know what will happen again if the government does not put its foot down and say it will come to an agreement with these people.
The company has said repeatedly through its spokesmen before the National Energy Board and before the special committee of this House that they do not want to begin the project unless they have the co-operation of the native people. They have said they do not want to build the pipeline in a hostile environment, and of course they do not. Too many things could happen. Too many difficulties could arise. I think we will regret not having had something much more definitive in this legislation with respect to an agreement in principle with the native people regarding their land claims in the areas affected by the pipeline.
The fourth thing I want to refer to has been referred to many times, but I want to touch on it because it was mentioned again today both by the Deputy Prime Minister and by the hon. member for Yukon. It is that there is no guarantee with reference to Canadian content. There is no guarantee of the 100,000 man-years of which the Deputy Prime Minister spoke, although actually if we take out the Dempster spur, we are probably talking about 67,000 or 68,000 man-years. However, that is a mere detail. The argument has been put up today, particularly by the hon. member for Yukon, who seemed to be more vociferous in protecting the government than the Deputy Prime Minister was, that we do not need to worry any more about Canadian content because we have the assurance of the company and the assurance of the government that they want to have Canadian content.

speechtext: And the committee.

And the
committee; there is no doubt that that is true. When Mr. Blair, the president of Foothills (Yukon) Limited, was on the stand, I quoted to him his own submission to the National Energy Board in which he said that they would buy all their pipe in Canada. I asked Mr. Blair if he still stood by that, and he said "yes". I asked if that applied to practically all the compressors, the fittings and the valves, and he said "yes". I believe him, and I believe the Deputy Prime Minister when he says he wants to see all the business done in Canada. But that is not the point at issue. The point at issue is that we are ratifying an agreement with the United States, and article 7 of that agreement is paramount. It says:
Having regard to the objectives of this agreement, each government will endeavour to ensure that the supply of goods and services to the Pipeline project will be on generally competitive terms. Elements to be taken into account in weighing competitiveness will include price, reliability, servicing capacity and delivery schedules.
April 4, 1978

That is crystal clear. The matter of competitiveness will not be decided on the pious wishes of the Deputy Prime Minister or the good intentions of the president of Foothills. The allocation of a contract in the final analysis will lie with the terms that are set out in article 7. When the hon. member for Yukon argues, as he did this afternoon, that one did not have to worry about this because a committee was going to be set up to which matters would be referred and that members of that committee would see to it that Canadian content was taken care of, could anything be more absurd? Did the hon. member take a look at what the proposed change in the standing order says?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: You supported that view in the committee.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
My friend does not need to worry about what 1 supported. If he would just try to control himself, I will get around to the position I took in committee. The proposal, which is in the order paper for today, is one which I certainly support. I support it in that it is better than having no committee at all, that it is a committee to which the monitoring agency must give account. The motion reads as follows:
"(t) Northern pipelines, to consist of not more than 15 members, to which shall stand permanently referred all reports, orders, agreements, regulations, directions and approvals mentioned in sections 12, 13, 14, 15 and 22 of the Northern Pipeline Act; provided that the said committee shall report thereon at least three times in every session.
What power does that give the committee? This is a committee to which the monitoring agency will periodically give information on how things are going. There is no guarantee that the reports it makes to parliament will even be discussed and certainly they will have no authority to discuss anything prior to it taking place.
One of my main quarrels with this legislation is that prior to its being suggested there was no accountability at all. Here was an agency which was to have the power of several departments, which was to have the power to authorize the expenditure of billions of dollars, which is responsible to no one, and which is not required to account to anyone. I supported the idea of having a committee of the House-certainly it is better than nothing-but it is a committee which deals with the matter after the fact, not prior to policies being instituted. For instance, they will not have a budget to discuss before the budget is made up. They may be allowed to look at expenditures after they have been made.

This will not give parliament any power. It is a reporting agency. It is certainly better than nothing, but let nobody think for a moment that this answers the problem of Canadian content in the pipeline. It does not at all. The matter of Canadian content is determined by the treaty, and as the hon. member for Yukon said this afternoon, you cannot amend a treaty. Of course you can. You can ask the government to go back and renegotiate the treaty as it did with the Columbia River
Northern Pipeline
Treaty. As the treaty now stands, there is no guarantee whatsoever that Canadian content will be properly recognized.
It may be that I am a born optimist-although sometimes my optimism is not fully warranted-but I think that the 88 cent dollar will probably help us more than any other thing the government might do, and we might get a fair share of the business. As my colleague, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), pointed out this afternoon, we should not forget that the Alyeska line was built entirely with Japanese pipe, and we should not forget that the Americans have the Disc program and that West German bankers have announced they are prepared to help finance any pipeline companies without interest charges during the construction period. We should not forget these things.
The hon. member for Yukon again said that my colleague, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, was being hypocritical when he talked about what GATT would do. GATT is a fact, but I point out that in the committee the minister and the law officer of the Crown were telling us that GATT did not really matter because in interpreting article 7 you must look at the preamble of the treaty under which the interests of both countries were to be advanced. So that GATT is not anything they can hide behind. The fact is that it would have been comparatively simple to have said to the Americans: "You want a land bridge across our country. It is going to cost us a great deal of inconvenience, it will impose some hardships upon our people; but it will create jobs and we want those jobs, so part of the quid pro quo is that we get the preference." We could have safeguarded the company and we could have said that Canadian contractors will be the first to bid. If the company can convince the minister in charge of the monitoring agency and the officers of the agency that those bids are out of line, then those bids could be swept aside and the whole project could be laid open to competitive bidding.

Almost every provincial government in this country with reference to highway contracts and public works contracts gives its own employers and its own workers a preference, so there is no reason at all why the Canadian government could not have done the same.

What I want to do in closing is to point out to the House that since we started to discuss this legislation the whole scenario has

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
changed. Originally we talked about a pipeline to take Prudhoe Bay gas to the United States.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Plus the Dempster.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Since that time, John G. McMillian, chief executive officer of the Northern Energy Company which is a partner of Foothills, has signed an agreement with the Pan-Alberta Gas Company for the purchase of 1.04 billion cubic feet of gas per day. That works out to something over 370 billion cubic feet of gas per year. That would mean an increase of 37 per cent in our exports of gas. I know that the answer will be that we cannot do this without the approval of the National Energy Board, but I say the National Energy Board will give that approval. I predict furthermore that they will get approval for even more gas than is now being requested.
It makes one ask whether this government is like the Bourbons who learned nothing and forget nothing. Have we forgotten that it is only five years ago that some of us were pleading in the House to phase out exports of oil? Today we are a net importer of oil and we are told by the National Energy Board that in the 1990's we will be spending $4 billion or $5 billion per year to pay for imports of oil. Are we going to make the same mistake with reference to gas? We are exporting 60 per cent of our gas production. We are going to increase it now by almost 40 per cent.
The government say: "Just a moment, we are going to work out a swap arrangement". I think a swap arrangement could be worked out if it were on an energy equivalent, so that for every 100 units of BTU energy we sold we would get back a similar amount, if and when we wanted it. That is what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources talked about a few months ago. The tune has now changed. When Mr. Bob Blair, the president of Foothills, appeared before the committee, I asked him about the swap. He said, "Yes, we would like to do that." I asked on what basis. He said in effect: "The only basis would be that we would sell Alberta gas down this pipeline to the United States, and if and when we needed gas, we would get it back; but we would sell at the going price now and we would buy it at the going price then." I am not saying the government will approve that, but I tried to get the chairman of the National Energy Board, when he was before the committee, to be very specific and he ducked right around the question. Certainly the Deputy Minister was not any more helpful.
Do we realize what we are doing? We are walking blindfolded into a continental energy policy. The Americans have always wanted a continental energy policy, particularly when they ran short of energy. We are like the couple of brothers who went into town: one saved his money and did well, and the other one had a high old time until he was broke and then said, "Let's pool our resources". That is exactly what the United States is doing. We have supplies of gas. We can manage for quite a few years. But we do not have inexhaustible supplies. If

we enter into a swap arrangement by which we sell 370 billion cubic feet of gas per year at $2.16 at the border, and 10 or 15 years down the road we buy it back at $3.50 or $4 per thousand cubic feet, we will have sold Canadians down the river. This House had better be aware of the manner in which the pieces are falling into place.
Now they are talking about starting the pipeline at the south end and building it so that it will take Alberta gas down to the United States, and the companies involved will make enough money out of that to finance in part the rest of the pipeline. The primary purpose in the immediate future is not to take Prudhoe Bay gas to the United States. The primary purpose is to take Alberta gas to the United States, and then hope some day, when the line is completed and Prudhoe Bay gas is coming down, if we need it, we can buy it back at a price. I suggest with great conviction that price will not be the same price we got for the gas we sold.
As I come to the end of my parliamentary life, I hate to make such a pessimistic speech; but I suggest to the hon. members of this House that my pessimism regarding this piece of legislation is based on some very bitter experience. I was in the House in 1962 when the Columbia River Treaty was debated. It was proposed by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). Also I was in the House in 1963 when we debated the amended version of it, as it was introduced by the government of the late Lester B. Pearson. There were only a few of us who fought that legislation. We were branded as holding up a necessary project. It was said that this was an opportunity to get the people of British Columbia very cheap gas, almost free gas, with very little inconvenience.
Of course, the legislation was shoved through, although we held it up for some months in the House and in committee. We were chastised in many parts of British Columbia for so doing. Today it is acknowledged by the government of British Columbia, headed by the son of the man who was premier when the agreement was signed, that the Columbia River Treaty has cost British Columbia over $500 million. We are much wiser now than we were then about the Columbia River Treaty.
Also I remember that in 1965, the government of the late Lester B. Pearson, brought in the Canada-United States auto pact. The same story was told then. This pact was going to give us more work and a larger share of the automobile manufacturing industry. It was going to remove the differential in price between cars in the United States and cars in Canada. What has happened? Again we opposed that legislation, but not because we were against the principle. It was because this legislation had all the cards stacked against Canada. We were shooting craps with loaded dice. It was rammed through, amid the cheers and the hurrahs by those who favoured it and the jeers for those who dare to question it. In the past 12 years, there has been a slight surplus in our favour in three of those years, but in nine of those years we have lost approximately $1 billion a year on that agreement. Surely we should have learned something.
April 4, 1978

I hope I am wrong this time. I hope this legislation will be beneficial and the pipeline will go well. I hope the agreements with the provinces, the territorial council and the native Indians will be the kind of agreements which protect Canadians. I hope the government will be able to work out ways to get around article 7 so that the Canadian content will give us the jobs we hope for. But I am very doubtful. Hon. members of the House should realize that if the harmful things which could happen do happen, they should never claim they were not warned.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues from the Edmonton area have not participated in this debate at any great length by deliberate policy. First of all, there was limited access to the committee. Also there was a desire to have an orderly debate without any protraction. If there is a city and a district which has a vital interest in this pipeline, certainly it is that portion of central and northern Alberta which is headquartered through the city of Edmonton.
At this time it is not my intention to engage in great polemics with regard to this pipeline, but we have to look at the general principles involved. I have listened with some care to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and earlier today to his colleague, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes). I am not going to engage in any point by point argument with either of those hon. members. They are expressing doctrinaire points of view which clearly indicate their socialistic views regarding the development and the operation of that industry or the use of resources. They betray the socialist traditional leaning by which they know better how to run affairs than the people who will be risking their money and energy developing these resources.
This is implicit. In fact, I would say it is explicit in the descriptions by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands of this House committee which has been appointed under the bill as a watchdog committee. As far as the socialists are concerned, this is not to be a watchdog committee in any way but, rather, it is to be a management committee. Those members will substitute their valued judgments regarding the construction of this pipeline for those of management and the people on the site who have the responsibility for the business commitment to build this pipeline, and the responsibility for the risk involved to their own money as well as the money of other investors. There is to be no government money involved in this particular project, and I hope that turns out to be the case.
I intend to propose something that has not been discussed so far during this debate, and this will involve what I consider to be the advantages to Canadian investors and how we can encourage them to provide the bulk of the money required for that part of the line going through Canada, without the necessity to resort to government participation.
Northern Pipeline
Some people will suggest that this project involves an extremely large investment requirement. Let me remind them that this is not to be financed entirely over one year. This pipeline will take some time to build, and investment will not only come from individual Canadians but from Canadian corporations as well.
I want to look at this project from a positive angle. We have heard hon. members often in the past describe many projects in a negative fashion. They have said almost everything about how not to achieve a project, and they have done so in detail. The people in the region from which I come have an entirely different concept about this project, as do the people from those regions represented in the past by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands.
I recall when that hon. gentleman was premier of the province of Saskatchewan. At that time there was very active petroleum development in the province of Alberta. If any government went about the development of oil and gas within provincial boundaries in a backward, hesitant, wrong-headed, impossible way, it was that administration led by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. As a result, entire fields of leases were given up, in total disgust, because of the conditions imposed by that socialist administration. The net result was that a great part of the population of Saskatchewan moved to Alberta where the oil and gas development action was, and they have remained there. Even today many people from Saskatchewan are moving to Alberta. That province has a different philosophy and a different approach. It has a positive approach, and that is the kind of outlook I want to see on the part of Canadians toward this project.
I have here a numer of magazines, including the Oil Week, which indicate advance proposals for the development of oil-sands mines in the constituency of my friend the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk). The next project will cost in the neighbourhood of $4 billion and will lead to the production of $150,000 barrels a day by 1985. Others are to follow.
We do not have the people or the materials to undertake more than one development of this type at a time. These are fantastically large projects. To the extent they are financed by Canadians, using Canadian materials and labour, we will have economic development for the benefit of Canadians. The governments of the provinces involved, whether they be of Saskatchewan or Alberta, and the Government of Canada will gain greater revenues through these developments which can be used to provide better services for Canadian citizens. Governments have an interest in these projects as well as the people, but they have to be initiated by private investment.
Governments lay down the guidelines and parameters of proper conduct for the development of these resources, but beyond that governments should not interfere. When listening to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on what I consider in many ways to be nitpicking matters, I was reminded of a couple of philosophers of the Middle Ages arguing about how many angels one could fit on the head of a pin. These are totally sterile arguments. After all, the proof of the pudding is in the eating, and the oil development policy of
4148

April 4, 1978
Northern Pipeline
the hon. gentleman when he was premier of Saskatchewan does not give me any proof or encouragement that what he describes could result from the sensible development of the oil industry. I suspect that this would accomplish quite the contrary, particularly since the industry in Saskatchewan has never recovered.
Let me speak a little bit about the capitalization of this project. The method of capitalization should not be covered by the bill as it is not covered in the agreement. I do not think one should establish capitalization by statutory requirement. I want to see Canadians participate in the capitalization and the ownership of shared capital, or debt capital, for this undertaking to the maximum extent possible.
To do that, Mr. Speaker, we are going to have to see a change in our tax laws. Our income tax law with its capital gains provision is an absolute albatross around the neck of any potential Canadian investor in projects of this kind. I do not care whether they are private individuals, whether they are corporate investors or whether they are actively engaged in the development and production of oil or gas in this country.
Over the past 20 years our history with regard to income tax as it relates to resource development is a woeful chapter of wrong-headed philosophy. It was designed-I do not know by whom or for what reason-to penalize the Canadian investor. There was an infamous principle occupation rule, which I have spoken against for over 15 years in this House. I must say in that regard that the government which I suppported was just as deaf to arguments and supplications on behalf of the oil industry while all the time Canadians, and particularly Albertans, were being driven out of ownership of the oil lands because our American counterparts could always bid us out. In the purchase of speculative leases, farm out agreements and all other related development work, we as Canadians simply could not recover any losses unless our principal occupation was the search for and development of oil and gas. Therefore, Canadian investors, be they doctors, lawyers, garage owners, farmers or what-have-you, could not put up $10,000 or $40,000 or any portion of the drilling costs, which were extremely low drilling costs for those earlier wells.
I have been through this many times in this House, Mr. Speaker. It was a one-shot affair for so many of them because if the net result of drilling a hole in the early days was a dry hole the loss was no more than $75,000 to $85,000. Rarely did it go to $100,000. But it was a loss and it could not be offset against any other income.
On the other hand, our American counterparts could always offset those losses against their other income. It was all right if you had enough money in the syndicate for one small company to drill three or four wells and you had a couple of producers, because you could always offset the expenses of the dry holes against the revenues earned by the producers. Now, however, that nefarious rule is gone and there can be a progressive write-off of those expenses.

How are we going to interest Canadians in such projects? Well, we all know what was done with the building of Alberta Gas Trunk back in the mid-1950's when the reservations for equity stock were limited to all Albertan citizens. But that policy in the 1950's before we had capital gains tax was geared to cupidity and the love of profit by the many thousands of Alberta citizens who took a reservation for the maximum number of shares that would be allotted to them and at the same time signed a trust agreement for which they were paid a bonus in order to assign the stock as soon as they got it. There was no limitation on the devolution of stock, and the net result was that soon the ownership of Alberta Gas Trunk passed out of the hands of Albertans. It is now a company that is controlled basically by investment funds of one kind or another.
How can we avoid that this time? Well, I am going to suggest that with the advent of the capital gains tax there is a method that will see that the classes of Canadians who will invest in this stock are such that the stock will remain in Canadian hands. It is simply this: that the income tax Act be amended to provide that, in the development and production of natural resources, there be created a so-called "ball park" of qualifying operations. If any Canadian taxpayer that is a Canadian citizen residing in Canada or a company controlled by Canadians is to invest in such stocks and was to keep the stock for a period of five years and then dispose of it, there would be a forgiveness of any capital gains tax. That is for five years. If it were kept for four years, then the forgiveness would be 80 per cent, and progressively moved downwards so that if the stock were kept within the "ball park" of investment there would only be a 20 per cent forgiveness.
There would, as I say, be the opportunity for rollover providing the stocks or the investments were kept within the category of qualifying investments, but one has to be a Canadian to get that advantage. It does not mean that non-Canadians could not invest, but such non-Canadians investing in Canada would have to pay income tax as well as capital gains tax. Of course, I am looking to an operation where basically we are going to see some profit and an increase in the value of those stocks or investments. To me the idea is fundamentally simple and would encourage Canadians to invest in this type of stock.
Now, how do we guarantee that the initial investment shall be for Canadians? This can be done the same way as it was done in the case of Alberta Gas Trunk, except that in that case Albertans had a monopoly on the initial offering. In this particular instance I dare say that since the pipeline would have to go through three areas of Canada-the Yukon, British Columbia and Alberta-some equitable formula could be found, perhaps on the basis of the proportion of total costs, and that percentage could be allocated to Albertans, a remaining percentage to British Columbia and then some percentage to the Yukon. To the extent that the people from any one province or zone did not take up the investment allotted to that zone, then that portion could fall to other Canadians; there are a number. I am not going to be dogmatic about the formula
April 4, 1978

except as to the insistence that it should be Canadians or Canadian companies who shall have the benefit of the bonuses with regard to this investment in this particular pipeline operation.
I do not know just what volume of savings would be forthcoming from Canadians. I would hope that they could take up the bulk of this offer over the period of years which this pipeline will require for construction. I would like to see this kind of financing applicable in some of the other developments in Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.
Let us start with resources and get the control of resources back into the hands of Canadians to a greater degree than is the case today. Goodness only knows that our tax policy over the years has driven the ownership of our natural resources, minerals, petroleum and natural gas, into the hands of foreign nationals or international companies. This has happened simply because they have the tax advantage. If there ever was an ostrich-like attitude toward this thing over the years, it was that of the Canadian government as well as some of the provincial administrations.
I am astounded that we, as a Canadian public, have put up with it this long and have failed to recognize how we could deal with the situation when the tools for it were immediately at hand. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that those things that require to be done with regard to the further implementation of the agreement concerning this pipeline shall be carried out and some of the many difficulties that exist will be ironed out.
I have not spoken about the settlement of Indian land claims. I do not think those were in any way related to the development of this pipeline, no more than they were related to the development of the Great Canadian Oil Sands, or Syncrude. Nor will they be related to the next consortia in Alberta or Saskatchewan with regard to the development of oil and gas. The claims arise for other reasons and shall be paid for by Canadians, because it is the government on behalf of Canadians which has the obligation with regard to land claims. I thought it was patently nonsensical for anyone to insist that part of the price of this agreement should be the setting aside of a fund of hundreds of millions of dollars to be paid for by the users of the gas to settle land claims. What nonsense. It has no relationship whatsoever. It is merely an attempt by someone who feels that there is a legitimate claim by the native peoples to find a suitable milk cow to provide the milk, as long as that person did not own the cow and did not have to feed the cow.
I hope that the Canadian government and any other provincial government which is involved in land claims will get on with the business. That is a matter of justice vis-a-vis the native peoples. It has nothing to do with the development of natural resources.
1 think that the Berger Commission in effect did a great disservice to the people of the Northwest Territories and along the Mackenzie River valley. Go there now and talk to them. Talk to the people of northern Alberta and British Columbia
Northern Pipeline
who have contact with the Northwest Territories and see what has happened and what is going to happen to what have been thriving communities as a result of the negative stand taken by the Berger commission. This was in effect an engineered affair. It was an engineered affair subject to points of view organized by the CBC and other people who used native associations, not for the benefit of those native associations, but for political purposes. In all that has happened the Berger report will join as quickly as possible other government reports on some lonely shelf in some back room. In my estimation, Mr. Speaker, that is its fate. It started out with the wrong concept and it finished with the wrong recommendations.
I commend, Mr. Speaker, the work that was done by my colleague from the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) on this particular bill and as a matter of fact by all members of the House who participated. I may disagree with the views of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, but I do not disagree with his own bona fides and his own earnestness. We can now get on with the final determination on this particular bill and I would invite hon. members to join in the support of third reading.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: POST OFFICE-DELIVERY SERVICE TO NEW SUBDIVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) said that he had just arrived from a visit in Edmonton, which is in the vicinity of my constituency. He was replying to a question put by me representing, as I do, the constituency of Saskatoon-Biggar. I ask if the Postmaster General does not know where Saskatoon is, because I suggest we have very serious problems with respect to our postal service. Many people in Saskatoon really believe that the Postmaster General does not know where Saskatoon is. I can assure him that by the end of this speech he will know exactly where it is and exactly what the problem is. I expect in turn that after having received this kind of advice he will do me and the people of Saskatoon, and generally people in urban communities across this country who deserve a reasonable postal service, the favour of providing door to door delivery. I hope he will have the presence of mind to stand up tonight and tell those people that they can expect now to receive the same kind of service or, to be more correct, door to door delivery service in the new subdivisions, a delivery service which they so sadly lack now.
Although it is tempting to blame the fact that the Postmaster General does not know where Saskatoon is as being the root problem of our inadequate mail service, the real malaise lies much deeper than that. Last week we faced yet another increase in the price of stamps in this country, sending the cost of mailing a first class letter up to an all-time high of 14 cents. It can come as little comfort to know that none of this money whatsoever will go toward improving service, and further that it will not even wipe out the Post Office's massive deficit.
I want to mention, for the benefit of the Postmaster General, some of the new areas in Saskatoon which require that service. They are: Meadow Green, Wildwood, Confederation Park, River Heights and Pacific Heights. Saskatonians living in these new areas will have to pay up like everyone else for the privilege of receiving mail weeks late, sometimes in deplorable condition. However, unlike Saskatonians living in older areas, they will have to trudge down to their little green boxes to get it. It is all part of this new service at the higher rate.
The Postmaster General said that he was sorry. He stated the following:
The Post Office Department is very conscious of the annoyance, inconvenience and disappointment caused to new home owners across Canada who expected to have door to door delivery of mail.
This was contained in a letter addressed to me and also to the city council of the city of Saskatoon. He has done nothing about it. We make out petitions and send them to the Postmaster General, and then he sends back a form letter of apology and attempts to provide more little green boxes. The form letters imply that the lack of door to door service is merely a temporary inconvenience. Don't bet on it! The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated last year that the government has given serious consideration to doing away with door to door delivery altogether. Thus, not only will the people in new areas

(Mr. Deputy Speaker.]
April 4, 1978

be deprived of this service; it will include every citizen and resident of this country. The Prime Minister has put on record that he is considering this option. Is this the type of service we can expect at higher prices for delivery of first class and other classes of mail?
The Post Office has now gone through a decade of drift, with only one consistent theme: a steady deterioration of service. It has the worst labour relations in the public service. It is losing over $1 billion of the taxpayers' money. It takes longer today to deliver mail than it did before the last war. It does not provide full service to those families who have a right to it. The service requires reform now, if it is not to slide into total chaos. For this reason, the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) established a special task force which will bring back its recommendations soon. After the next election, the Conservative government will make a new start in the Post Office. It needs it. What does the Postmaster General propose to do now for those people who have been deprived wrongfully for over two years of their right to have door to door delivery service?

subtopic: POST OFFICE-DELIVERY SERVICE TO NEW SUBDIVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could argue with many of the affirmations stated by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn), but I prefer a more positive approach to the problem, and I should like to tell hon. members of the House what we intend to do.
Yesterday the hon. member asked about the lifting of the current freeze on extensions of letter carrier service and the possibilities of alternatives. I have been discussing the matter with senior departmental officials, but basically I can restate only what I outlined on previous occasions.
The Post Office Department has several methods of getting mail to the public. One of the most common methods is that of the individual picking up his mail from a post office box in a small town post office, in his apartment building or in a large business complex. Another is by general delivery over the counter, and still another is by rural route delivery.
In most cases both businesses and residences in cities enjoy door to door service. While this method of delivery is relatively efficient in business areas, the cost per item of mail delivered in the residential areas is relatively high. It would be well to realize that in 1978 the milkman, breadman and dry cleaner have eliminated daily service in most residential areas. Obviously they are faced with the same high cost of delivery as we are.
In 1972 the Post Office had a $90 million deficit. The projected deficit this year, without the rate increase, would have been $717 million, and for 1980 it would have been $1 billion. This situation was assessed in November 1975, and it was determined that there were just not enough funds in taxpayers' pockets to handle these rapidly increasing costs. In the name of good administration and sound business practices, the government restrained its spending. The only alternative was to put a freeze on the extension of door to door delivery service.
Adjournment Debate
In place of door-to-door service, new suburban areas were provided delivery service through the use of group mail boxes located on the side of the streets adjacent to these new areas, bearing in mind that the Canadian citizen is entitled to the services of the mails.

I realize that city dwellers are used to door-to-door delivery service. I realize also that in some neighbourhoods we are putting some hardship on our customers by forcing them to pick up their mail at the wickets of general delivery post office or at a group of mail boxes located near their homes.

I realize, however, that I have the serious responsibility of providing Canadians with a mail delivery service which has some degree of consistency, yet in doing so I must ensure that excess costs are avoided.
I should like to reassure Canadians that for the moment there is no question of curtailing any existing services. If we are to contemplate any changes or expansion in delivery methods we must re-evaluate the overall situation and consult with the unions to obtain their full collaboration, keeping in mind that the taxpayer is the one who always foots the bill.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-MINISTER'S ACTION TO IMPROVE SERVICE AND LOW EMPLOYEE MORALE
POST OFFICE-MINISTER'S ACTION TO IMPROVE SERVICE AND LOW EMPLOYEE MORALE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) is with us tonight. The last time I dealt with matters on the motion to adjourn the spokesman was the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley), who completely missed the point I was making. Unfortunately the replies of the Postmaster General since he has assumed responsibility for this portfolio-and he is the tenth Postmaster General in the past six years-would indicate he is not yet aware of the gravity of the situation. The only response to some of the problems briefly outlined tonight by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has been to increase postal rates and to change postmasters general. This has only aggravated the problem.
The Post Office provides an essential service, but it is in desperate difficulty and its efficiency has been going downhill continually for ten years. This is demonstrated by the more than one half billion dollar deficit in the past fiscal year. Business is declining, particularly parcel post, the level of which today is down to the level of 20 years ago, and projections with regard to first class mail indicate this mail is down by one million pieces. The situation is desperate when periodical publishers in Canada, upon whom the Post Office depends for goodwill, are forced to go to court to get justice as a result of the service, or lack of it, by the Post Office Department. At the present time they have an appeal before the Supreme Court of Ontario.
The Postmaster General, in the face of these obvious problems, has told members of the House that service is improving,

April 4, 1978
Adjournment Debate
as are industrial relations. In a reply to the hon. member for Hamilton-West (Mr. Alexander) yesterday it was pointed out that you cannot even depend on registered mail these days. Obviously postal service is in a very desperate state of deterioration, and this is mainly the result of a disastrous breakdown in morale following the breakdown in labour-management relations.
I do not have much time to develop my theme, but it relates to mechanization and the failure of management to consult with unions when introducing this monster for the handling of our mail. There has been a complete breakdown in the parcel post sorting mechanism at the bulk mail facility at Gateway, Mississauga. The Post Office is establishing an emergency manual sorting process at the abandoned warehouse of Canadian Arsenals. It looks as if they are going to have to take the computer program back to contract. All these things are evidence that something drastic has got to be done.
Canada is not unique. The Conservative party have a task force working on this matter. We have already come to a lot of positive conclusions and I am going to pass some positive tips on to the Postmaster General tonight. The United Kingdom, West Germany and Japan, all modern states, have faced exactly the same problem. Several of them have gone the route of the Crown corporation because, after all, the modern post office is an industrial organization. However, essentially they have dealt with the problems of management and labour relations in the post office by establishing management advisory committees where management, workers, postal users and customers sit around the same table.
It is not consultation or co-determination or comteam, or any such terms that are used by those who think they are resolving the problems in Canada's Post Office. It is constant consultation. No decision is made in dealing with the major problems in our changing technology in the post office unless consensus is achieved. As a result, you have harmonious co-operation and you have every aspect of the postal service working together to achieve the most efficient operation possible.
The union have offered the Postmaster General an alternative. They say they want a study. They want the Postmaster General and the government to consider the possibility of a Crown corporation. Why does he not move in this direction? He will never get a contract unless he does something. To do nothing is to court continued disaster. Leadership is desperately and urgently needed. There must be legislative action, and this is the question I raised the other day. The Postmaster General said: "Maybe before the election, maybe after the election". After the election will be too late. This is the voice of management!
I have before me a report known as the Uberig report. It is dated August 11, 1975, and it has excellent suggestions for improving the post office situation. The information paper is headed: "Re. Special Status For the Canada Post Office". Recommendations have been made by the union to improve

the situation. The postal users have gone to court to get justice from the Post Office Department, and certainly the voice of the general public protesting loud and clear has been heard in the land. I trust that the Postmaster General will indicate that he is going to take action, and that he is going to take it as quickly and as urgently as possible.

For example, he talks about harmony in the United States post office. He should read American newspapers, where he will find talk of the danger of strike in the post office and the talk-

It would be a good thing if the hon. member on the other side of the chamber would learn what has been done during the past few weeks. I will tell him what has been done during the past few weeks in the Post Office Department. I had meetings with all union leaders, including Mr. Parrot, president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. I have had meetings with all senior management in the Post Office Department as well as regional and divisional managers. The General Trade and Labour Union has ended its rotating strikes and an agreement has been reached. The Hubling commission got underway concerning allegations of mail disruptions during the Christmas period in Toronto. I have visited major and minor plants in the Toronto area and other places and have talked with many workers in order to determine exactly what they think.
Invitations have been made to CUPW to sit down and talk about labour problems. We have invited them to study with us the feasibility and possibility of creating a Crown corporation. We have also invited them to participate in our inter-group meetings. However, all the invitations fell on deaf ears and a response was never received.
Our objective is to negotiate an acceptable collective agreement with CUPW without a work disruption if at all possible. We have made efforts and every attempt to improve and strengthen our dialogue and our relations with the post office workers. We should communicate more and more with the employees, I agree, and with the general public so they can understand the situation and then be able to make a valid and

a more informed judgment on the situation. We will try to avoid an escalatory situation of power struggling. It is not a question of who is the strongest. When one talks about leadership, there is all kinds of leadership. We have leadership and we will show leadership.
