subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN PIPELINE-DISCUSSIONS ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN AREAS
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN PIPELINE-DISCUSSIONS ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 16 I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) the degree of involvement of his ministry with reference to the development of the Alaska pipeline. I did that on the basis of having participated in the extensive standing committee hearings on the pipeline and on the basis of having listened to speeches in the House on second reading and at report stage about the concerns of government with reference to industrial development along the course of the pipeline and in those communities which will be closely associated with the pipeline.
I have in fact addressed similar questions to the same minister before the standing committee dealing with regional economic expansion. The minister on March 16, in reply to me, indicated two things which are of concern. He indicated that there had been no negotiations with municipal authorities but that there had been some discussions, I must assume in a very shallow and vague fashion, with provincial authorities. He really was not quite correct because some of his officials in DREE in British Columbia have met with the regional district representatives in the northern part of British Columbia.
What really concerns me is that the minister, in his answer to me on March 16, went on to say that he was trying to put into force a subagreement on the industrial development of that province which was signed last year. Mr. Speaker, a careful analysis of the subagreements dealing with industry which were signed with British Columbia last year will indicate to the reader that those subagreements in no general or specific way deal with pipeline development and the need to develop the industrial sector along the course of that major undertaking.
In fact, on the occasion that I addressed the minister with reference to this issue before the standing committee, he did in both instances make reference to the service sector. I must assume, sir, that it is a reflection of the minister's thinking in general terms, in general policy, when he speaks of the service sector. The last thing that needs assistance is the service sector. The first thing that needs consideration is some orderly planning for the future in terms of the industrial community, whether it be in the manufacturing sense, basic industries, resource industries or secondary industry.
Adjournment Debate
I find it very regrettable that on the basis of questions that I have asked the minister both in the House and before the standing committee he is clearly not prepared to give his department the mandate to make the necessary planning, certainly in the long range, that is required if this pipeline is going to be more than simply a pipeline, which in itself is a major proposal. If it is going to serve in any real sense the needs of Canadians in the north, there has to be some planning. That planning falls within the responsibility of the minister. Clearly that minister is not prepared to live up to that responsibility.
I can only suggest that a different government, a Conservative government, would have that planning in place so that when we go into this proposal four years down the line we would know what provisions can be made for industry and what provisions the government would have to make to encourage industry to develop. It would not be to live up to some willy-nilly development along the fringes of the pipeline which inevitably in the long haul will fail, and not to provide dollars to the service sector when it is clearly not needed.
I hope the minister will study the comments I have made and will give his officials a mandate to work in the direction I have suggested, other than the type of summary that DREE has provided with reference to the pipeline debate, which had some value but clearly did not deal with that particular mandate of that minister.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN PIPELINE-DISCUSSIONS ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to reply on behalf of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) for whom I had the pleasure of being parliamentary secretary for 12 months prior to being Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance.
It is not accurate to state that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has not taken any initiative to discuss economic development with municipal and regional officials in northern British Columbia. The officials have had frequent discussions and have made frequent presentations to various municipal and regional bodies, chambers of commerce, etc., in northern British Columbia, including Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John and Fort Nelson. In fact it was the recognition of the potential for economic development in the northern part of the province that led the department to the decision to establish an office in Prince George, which would make staff and programs more accessible to the people and needs of northern British Columbia.
The officials have not undertaken, not is it their place to undertake, discussions specific to the proposed northern pipeline with such bodies. As the hon. member is aware, the responsible minister for the northern pipeline is the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and the responsible agency is the Northern Pipeline Agency.
The department has contributed significantly to both the collection of information required for pipeline discussions in British Columbia and negotiations between the pipeline com-

April 4, 1978
Adjournment Debate
missioner's office and officials of the provincial government in British Columbia.
The hon. member knows the negotiations between the federal and provincial governments having to do with the pipeline are not yet concluded, and as a result it would be inappropriate for the department either to discuss details of the pipeline with regional planning bodies or to negotiate possible subagreements having to do with the pipeline with provincial officials until the pipeline negotiations are completed.
As the minister stated in his reply to the hon. member on March 16, 1978, the industrial development subsidiary agreement is being applied in northern British Columbia. Industrial commissions under the subagreement have been agreed to in a number of places, including the Fort St. John area, and the department has received a number of applications under the small business program from the area, some having been approved. Others are under active consideration at this time. In addition, the department is currently giving consideration to several RDIA applications from northern British Columbia in addition to those already approved.
I understand the minister will be announcing this week a fairly substantial grant under the special ARDA program in that part of the country. I should also state that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the provincial government contributed some funds under the industrial development subsidiary agreement toward the cost of holding the "Impact '78" conference which recently took place in Fort St. John at the initiative of interested groups in the northeast, to examine economic development issues in the region. This meeting was attended by the newly-appointed northern district B.C. manager of DREE. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, while DREE officials are not, for the reason stated, actively negotiating with municipal and regional officials relative to the pipeline, the department is very active in northern British Columbia and will continue to be active in promoting its economic development.
